Ulam Sets in New Settings

Tej Bade Address: Phillips Exeter Academy, Exeter, NH 03833 Email address: tbade@exeter.edu , Kelly Cui Address: Leland High School, San Jose, CA 95120 Email address: kcui930@gmail.com , Antoine Labelle Address: Collège de Maisonneuve, Montreal, Quebec, Canada Email address: e1995364@cmaisonneuve.qc.ca, antoinelab01@gmail.com and Deyuan Li Address: Yale University, New Haven, CT 06511 Email address: deyuan.li@yale.edu
Abstract.

The classical Ulam sequence is defined recursively as follows: a1=1a_{1}=1, a2=2a_{2}=2, and ana_{n}, for n>2n>2, is the smallest integer not already in the sequence that can be written uniquely as the sum of two distinct earlier terms. This sequence is known for its mysterious quasi-periodic behavior and its surprising rigidity when we let a2a_{2} vary. This definition can be generalized to other sets of generators in different settings with a binary operation and a valid notion of size. Since there is not always a natural linear ordering of the elements, the resulting collections are called Ulam sets. In this paper, we study Ulam sets in new settings. First, we investigate the structure of canonical Ulam sets in free groups; this is the first investigation of Ulam sets in noncommutative groups. We prove several symmetry results and prove a periodicity result for eventually periodic words with fixed prefixes. Then, we study Ulam sets in ℤ×(ℤ/n​ℤ)\mathbb{Z}\times(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}) and prove regularity for an infinite class of initial sets. We also examine an intriguing phenomenon about decompositions of later elements into sums of the generators. Finally, we consider 𝒱\mathcal{V}-sets, a variant where the summands are not required to be distinct; we focus on 𝒱\mathcal{V}-sets in ℤ2\mathbb{Z}^{2}.

1. Introduction

1.1. Background

In 1964, Stanislaw Ulam [16] introduced the following curious sequence of natural numbers: the first two elements are 11 and 22, and then we repeatedly choose the next element (in a greedy way) to be the smallest integer not already in the sequence that can be represented uniquely as the sum of two distinct previous elements. The first few terms are

1,2,3,4,6,8,11,13,16,18,26,….1,2,3,4,6,8,11,13,16,18,26,\ldots.

This “classical” Ulam sequence is known to be quite chaotic, but it also exhibits very intriguing phenomena. Although the sequence appears to behave quite randomly, Steinerberger [15] observed a “hidden signal”: there seems to exist a real number λ≈2.4434\lambda\approx 2.4434 such that the Ulam sequence is far from uniformly distributed modulo λ\lambda. Since the publication of Steinerberger’s result, the classical Ulam sequence has been the object of renewed attention [4, 5, 12, 13], but its behavior remains far from understood. Of course, one can obtain other Ulam sequences by starting with initial values other than 1,21,2. Some choices of initial values result in highly structured sequences [2, 3, 14], and others appear to result in highly irregular sequences like what appears in the classical Ulam sequence.

In 2018, Kravitz and Steinerberger [9] extended the notion of an Ulam sequence to settings other than the natural numbers, with the following caveat: when multiple elements have the same size, one is chosen arbitrarily to be added first. As a result, there can be no canonical notion of a sequence per se, and it makes more sense to study the unordered Ulam set. (The Ulam set arising from an initial set is well-defined as long as the notion of size satisfies some natural weak monotonicity conditions.) Kravitz and Steinerberger focused on Ulam sets in ℤd\mathbb{Z}^{d} (see also the work of [7]), and they suggested several other settings for studying Ulam sets. The purpose of the present paper is to initiate the study of several of these variants.

One such variant, for example, consists of Ulam sets in ℤ×(ℤ/n​ℤ)\mathbb{Z}\times(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}). In this setting, Ulam sets can exhibit rather surprising new behavior. For instance, whereas Ulam sets in ℤ\mathbb{Z} are always infinite, this is not always the case in ℤ×(ℤ/n​ℤ)\mathbb{Z}\times(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}). One example appears in ℤ×(ℤ/8​ℤ)\mathbb{Z}\times(\mathbb{Z}/8\mathbb{Z}), where the Ulam set generated by the initial set {(1,0),(1,1),(2,5)}\{(1,0),(1,1),(2,5)\} does not contain any points with xx-coordinate larger than 5151. We will show in Section 4.3 that if n<5n<5, then every Ulam set in ℤ×(ℤ/n​ℤ)\mathbb{Z}\times(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}) has infinitely many elements.

1.2. General definition of Ulam sets and 𝒱\mathcal{V}-sets

Following the setup from Theorem 2 of [9], we now formally define Ulam sets in general settings. Let GG be a group (written multiplicatively), and fix a finite subset S⊂GS\subset G (the initial set of generators). Let DSD_{S} denote the set of all elements of GG that can be expressed as a nonempty product of elements from SS. Suppose moreover that there exists a “size” function f:DS→ℝf:D_{S}\to\mathbb{R} such that f⁡(x​y)>max⁡{f⁡(x),f⁡(y)}f(xy)>\max\{f(x),f(y)\} for all x,y∈DSx,y\in D_{S}, and f−1((−∞,r])f^{-1}((-\infty,r]) is finite for all r∈ℝr\in\mathbb{R}. Then we define the Ulam set generated by S (written 𝒰⁡(S)\mathcal{U}(S)) as follows:

  1. (1)

    We put the elements of SS into 𝒰⁡(S)\mathcal{U}(S).

  2. (2)

    We then repeatedly add to 𝒰⁡(S)\mathcal{U}(S) the smallest (according to ff) element of DSD_{S} that is not already in 𝒰⁡(S)\mathcal{U}(S) and which is uniquely represented as the product of two distinct elements already in 𝒰⁡(S)\mathcal{U}(S). When there are multiple such smallest elements, we choose one to add arbitrarily.

As described in [9], since elements of SS affect the representations of only elements of greater size, valid elements of the same size can be added in 𝒰⁡(S)\mathcal{U}(S) in any arbitrary order without changing the resulting unordered set. When GG is abelian, we speak of sums rather than products and consider the representations x+yx+y and y+xy+x to be the same.

In [10], Kuca introduced a variant of Ulam sequences, called 𝒱\mathcal{V}-sequences, in which the summands in a representation are not required to be distinct. Similarly, we can define 𝒱\mathcal{V}-sets in the same way as Ulam sets, except that the multiplicands or summands are not required to be distinct. When the ambient setting is clear, we denote by 𝒱⁡(S)\mathcal{V}(S) the 𝒱\mathcal{V}-set generated by the initial set SS.

2. Main results

2.1. Ulam sets in free groups

We begin in Section 3 with Ulam sets in the free group F2F_{2}. We emphasize that this is the first ever investigation of Ulam sets in non-abelian groups. In order to have a suitable notion of size, we will restrict our attention to the “positive” part of F2F_{2}, i.e., the set of nonidentity elements that can be expressed without the use of 0−10^{-1} or 1−11^{-1}; this set can be identified with the set 𝒲2\mathcal{W}_{2} of finite nonempty binary strings, where multiplication is given by concatenation. Given w∈𝒲2w\in\mathcal{W}_{2}, we define f⁡(w)f(w) to be the length of ww.

We will focus on the case where the initial set SS contains only two elements; even this simple example exhibits substantially nontrivial phenomena. In particular, we study 𝒰⁡({0,1})\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}), the Ulam set generated by the canonical elements 00 and 11. The first few elements are

{0,1,01,10,001,011,100,110,…}.\{0,1,01,10,001,011,100,110,\ldots\}.

Note that 𝒰⁡({0,1})\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}) exhibits universal behavior for the case where SS consists of two elements v1,v2v_{1},v_{2} of the same size since the homomorphism sending 00 to v1v_{1} and 11 to v2v_{2} induces a bijection between the corresponding Ulam sets. We establish several symmetries of 𝒰⁡({0,1})\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}) and characterize the elements with exactly one 11.

Theorem 3.3.

Let u∈𝒲2u\in\mathcal{W}_{2} be a word of length nn with exactly one 11, and let ii be the index of that 11. The word uu is in 𝒰⁡({0,1})\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}) if and only if (n−1i−1)\binom{n-1}{i-1} is odd.

We also work towards understanding the elements with exactly two 11’s, and we show the somewhat surprising result that the gap between the 11’s in such a word cannot be too large. We then exhibit infinite periodic structures in 𝒰⁡({0,1})\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}) in a way somewhat akin to the “column phenomenon” from [9].

Finally, for the analogous 𝒱\mathcal{V}-set (where we don’t require the words forming a representation to be distinct), we find that whether or not a word is in 𝒱⁡({0,1})\mathcal{V}(\{0,1\}) depends only on its length. The first few elements of this 𝒱\mathcal{V}-set are

{0,1,00,01,10,11,0000,0001,…}.\{0,1,00,01,10,11,0000,0001,\ldots\}.

We find a simple characterization of all the elements of 𝒱⁡({0,1})\mathcal{V}(\{0,1\}):

Theorem 3.11.

A word uu of length nn is in 𝒱⁡({0,1})\mathcal{V}(\{0,1\}) if and only if nn is a power of 22.

2.2. Ulam sets in ℤ×(ℤ/n​ℤ)\mathbb{Z}\times(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})

In Section 4, we investigate Ulam sets in ℤ×(ℤ/n​ℤ)\mathbb{Z}\times(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}), where the notion of size is f⁡((,,,))=xf((x,y))=x (and we choose SS so that each element has strictly positive first coordinate). As discussed in [9], this setting is motivated by multiplicative Ulam sets in the complex numbers. Figure 1, for example, is the Ulam set 𝒰⁡({(1,0),(1,1)})\mathcal{U}(\{(1,0),(1,1)\}) in ℤ×(ℤ/7​ℤ)\mathbb{Z}\times(\mathbb{Z}/7\mathbb{Z}). We see that the set appears to exhibit chaotic behavior. It is not known whether this set is infinite or whether the density is the same in each row (when yy is fixed). Some other Ulam sets, however, can exhibit very structured properties.

We define the associated lattice of the Ulam set generated by {v1,⋯,vk}\{v_{1},\cdots,v_{k}\} to be the subgroup of ℤk\mathbb{Z}^{k} consisting of the solutions to the equation x1​v1+⋯+xk​vk=0x_{1}v_{1}+\cdots+x_{k}v_{k}=0. The structure of an Ulam set is uniquely determined by its associated lattice (see [9]), and it turns out that every Ulam set with two generators in an abelian group has the same associated lattice as that of an Ulam set in either ℤ2\mathbb{Z}^{2} or ℤ×(ℤ/n​ℤ)\mathbb{Z}\times(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}). Since the former setting has received attention previously in [9], our investigation in this sense rounds out the study of Ulam sets with two generators in abelian groups.

Finch [3] proved that an Ulam set in ℤ\mathbb{Z} with finitely many even elements is regular (eventually periodic). Similarly, we establish a necessary and sufficient condition for an Ulam set in ℤ×(ℤ/n​ℤ)\mathbb{Z}\times(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}) to be regular.

Theorem 4.2.

An Ulam set 𝒰\mathcal{U} in ℤ×(ℤ/n​ℤ)\mathbb{Z}\times(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}) is regular if and only if there exists some regular subset E⊂ℤ×(ℤ/n​ℤ)E\subset\mathbb{Z}\times(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}) such that the sum of two elements of EE is never in EE and only finitely many elements of 𝒰\mathcal{U} are not in EE.

In fact, Finch’s characterization is a special case of our result, obtained by taking n=1n=1 and EE to be the set of odd numbers.

Using these techniques, we show that Ulam sets with two generators and associated lattice generated by (−2,b)(-2,b) for b>3b>3 are regular, extending the work of Schmerl and Spiegel [14], who established the special case where bb is odd. These proofs are quite long and technical.

Since each element of an Ulam set (other than the elements of the generating set) has a unique representation as a sum of previous elements, it is possible to work backwards and keep track of overall decomposition into multiples of the original generators. We study these decompositions for Ulam sets in abelian groups with two generators and observe a very intriguing phenomenon: the ratio of the contributions of each generator is approximately the same for all elements. We show, as a weaker result, that the contributions of the two generators cannot be too skewed.

Finally, we investigate the conditions for an Ulam set in ℤ×(ℤ/n​ℤ)\mathbb{Z}\times(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}) to be finite. (Recall that every Ulam set in ℤd\mathbb{Z}^{d} is easily seen to be infinite.) As an example, the Ulam set 𝒰⁡{(1,0),(1,1),(2,5)}\mathcal{U}\{(1,0),(1,1),(2,5)\} in ℤ×(ℤ/8​ℤ)\mathbb{Z}\times(\mathbb{Z}/8\mathbb{Z}) is finite.

We show that if such an Ulam set is finite, then it must have at least 55 elements that assume the maximum value in the first coordinate.

Theorem 4.14.

Let 𝒰\mathcal{U} be a finite Ulam set in ℤ×(ℤ/n​ℤ)\mathbb{Z}\times(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}) and let xmaxx_{\max} be the greatest xx-coordinate of elements of 𝒰\mathcal{U}. Then 𝒰\mathcal{U} contains at least 55 elements of the form (xmax,y)(x_{\max},y).

In particular, this implies that for n<5n<5, all Ulam sets in ℤ×(ℤ/n​ℤ)\mathbb{Z}\times(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}) are infinite. Note that this is a tight bound since, for n≥5n\geq 5, the Ulam set 𝒰⁡({(1,0),(1,1),…,(1,n−2),(1,n−1)})\mathcal{U}(\{(1,0),(1,1),\ldots,(1,n-2),(1,n-1)\}) contains no element other than the generators.

2.3. Higher-dimensional 𝒱\mathcal{V}-sets

In Section 5, we study 𝒱\mathcal{V}-sets in ℤd\mathbb{Z}^{d}. Recall that a 𝒱\mathcal{V}-set is a variant of an Ulam set where the summands in the representations need not be distinct. Kravitz and Steinerberger [9] demonstrated a “column phenomenon” for certain Ulam sets in ℤ2\mathbb{Z}^{2}: if SS contains a single generator in the column x=0x=0, then, for each fixed value of xx, the set of values of yy such that (x,y)(x,y) is in 𝒰⁡(S)\mathcal{U}(S) is eventually periodic. An example of this behavior is shown in Figure 3.

We adapt their techniques to show that the same phenomenon persists for 𝒱\mathcal{V}-sets in ℤ2\mathbb{Z}^{2}.

Theorem 5.2.

Let 𝒮\mathcal{S} either be an Ulam set or a 𝒱\mathcal{V}-set in ℤ2\mathbb{Z}^{2} for which the column x=0x=0 is eventually periodic. Then all of the columns of 𝒮\mathcal{S} are eventually periodic.

Next, we study the “canonical” 𝒱\mathcal{V}-set in ℤ2\mathbb{Z}^{2} with the generating set {(0,1),(1,0)}\{(0,1),(1,0)\}. In contrast to the Ulam set setting, where starting with two generators in ℤ2\mathbb{Z}^{2} leads to simple lattice-like behavior, 𝒱⁡({(0,1),(1,0)})\mathcal{V}(\{(0,1),(1,0)\}) has a more complicated structure. We obtain an interesting result showing that it is not too chaotic.

Corollary 5.4.

Let

T={(1,1),(2,0),(0,2),(3,2),(2,3),(6,3),(3,6),(9,6),(6,9),(10,5),(5,10),(14,5),(5,14)}.T=\{(1,1),(2,0),(0,2),(3,2),(2,3),(6,3),(3,6),(9,6),(6,9),(10,5),(5,10),(14,5),(5,14)\}.

Then every element of 𝒱⁡({(0,1),(1,0)})\mathcal{V}(\{(0,1),(1,0)\}) outside of TT (and the generators) must use an element of TT in its (unique) representation as a sum of two previous elements.

Finally, in Section 6, we raise several open questions and suggest avenues for future research on Ulam sets in settings other than F2F_{2} and ℤd\mathbb{Z}^{d}.

3. Ulam sets in Free Groups

We begin by exhibiting a few elementary properties of 𝒰⁡({0,1})\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}).

3.1. Symmetries

Let uu be a word on the alphabet {0,1}\{0,1\}. We define the reverse of uu (denoted u¯\overline{u}) to be the word obtained by reversing the order of the characters in uu. We define the complement of uu (denoted u^\widehat{u}) to be the word obtained by changing all of the 00’s to 11’s and 11’s to 00’s.

Theorem 3.1.

A word u∈𝒲2u\in\mathcal{W}_{2} is contained in the Ulam set 𝒰⁡({0,1})\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}) if and only if u¯\overline{u} is also contained in 𝒰⁡({0,1})\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}). Similarly, u∈𝒰⁡({0,1})u\in\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}) if and only if u^∈𝒰⁡({0,1})\widehat{u}\in\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}).

Proof.

Because the two halves of the theorem are similar, we will be proving them in parallel. We proceed by induction on the length of uu. The base case is where uu has length 11. We know that the words of length 11 in 𝒰⁡({0,1})\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}) are precisely 00 and 11; in particular, the reverse and the complement of each of these words are also in the set. Now we proceed with the inductive step. Assume that if a word of length k<nk<n is in the Ulam set 𝒰⁡({0,1})\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}), then both its reverse and complement are also in 𝒰⁡({0,1})\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}). Let uu be a word of length nn in 𝒰⁡({0,1})\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}) with unique representation u=v∗wu=v*w (where v≠wv\neq w). Note that u¯=w¯∗v¯\overline{u}=\overline{w}*\overline{v} and u^=v^∗w^\widehat{u}=\widehat{v}*\widehat{w}, where v¯\overline{v}, w¯\overline{w}, v^,\widehat{v}, and w^\widehat{w} are in 𝒰⁡({0,1})\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}) by the inductive hypothesis. This shows that u¯\overline{u} and u^\widehat{u} each have at least one representation.

For the first statement, assume for the sake of contradiction that there exists a second representation u¯=y¯∗x¯\overline{u}=\overline{y}*\overline{x}, where x¯\overline{x} and y¯\overline{y} are distinct elements of 𝒰⁡({0,1})\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}) and, moreover, x¯≠v¯\overline{x}\neq\overline{v}. Since u¯=y¯∗x¯\overline{u}=\overline{y}*\overline{x}, we also have u=x∗yu=x*y, where x,y∈𝒰⁡({0,1})x,y\in\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}) by the inductive hypothesis (because xx and yy are strictly shorter than uu). However, this contradicts uu having a unique representation, so u¯\overline{u} must be in 𝒰⁡({0,1})\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}). For the second statement, we assume for the sake of contradiction that there exists a second representation u^=x^∗y^\widehat{u}=\widehat{x}*\widehat{y}, where x^,y^∈𝒰⁡({0,1})\widehat{x},\widehat{y}\in\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}) and x^≠v^\widehat{x}\neq\widehat{v}. Since u^=x^∗y^\widehat{u}=\widehat{x}*\widehat{y}, we also have u=x∗yu=x*y, where x,y∈𝒰⁡({0,1})x,y\in\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}) by the inductive hypothesis. Once again, this contradicts uu having a unique representation, so u^∈𝒰⁡({0,1})\widehat{u}\in\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}). ∎

We define a palindrome to be a word pp such that p=p¯p=\overline{p}.

Corollary 3.2.

The only palindromes of odd length in 𝒰⁡({0,1})\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}) are 00 and 11.

Proof.

Let pp be a palindrome with odd length other than 00 and 11. In particular, pp has length at least 33. We will show that the existence of one representation of pp as the concatenation of two distinct previous elements of 𝒰⁡({0,1})\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}) implies the existence of another such representation of pp. Suppose p=u∗vp=u*v, where u,v∈𝒰⁡({0,1})u,v\in\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}). By Theorem 3.1, the elements u¯\overline{u} and v¯\overline{v} must also be in 𝒰⁡({0,1})\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}). Since pp is a palindrome, it may also be represented as p=p¯=v¯∗u¯p=\overline{p}=\overline{v}*\overline{u}, where v¯≠u\overline{v}\neq u since uu and vv must have different lengths as pp has odd length. Therefore, pp cannot be in 𝒰⁡({0,1})\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}). ∎

3.2. Characterizing words with a small number of 11’s

We have demonstrated symmetries among words in 𝒰⁡({0,1}).\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}). Now we focus on figuring out whether a specific word is in the set based on its actual sequence of 00’s and 11’s. Specifically, we begin with words with a small number of 11’s. Because of Theorem 3.1, this discussion also pertains to words with a small number of 00’s. We define the index of a letter in a word to be the number of letters to its left (including the letter itself).

Theorem 3.3.

Let u∈𝒲2u\in\mathcal{W}_{2} be a word of length nn with exactly one 11, and let ii be the index of that 11. The word uu is in 𝒰⁡({0,1})\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}) if and only if (n−1i−1)\binom{n-1}{i-1} is odd.

Proof.

Once again, we proceed with induction on the length of the word. The base case is where uu has length 11 or 22. The only word of length 11 in 𝒲2\mathcal{W}_{2} with exactly one 11 is 11. In this case, n=1n=1, i=1,i=1, (00)=1\binom{0}{0}=1 is odd, and the element 11 is in fact in 𝒰⁡({0,1})\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}). The words of length 22 in 𝒲2\mathcal{W}_{2} with exactly one 11 are 0101 and 1010. For the former, n=2n=2, i=2i=2, (11)=1\binom{1}{1}=1 is odd, and 0101 is in 𝒰⁡({0,1}).\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}). For the latter, n=2n=2, i=1i=1, (10)=1\binom{1}{0}=1 is odd, and 1010 is also in 𝒰⁡({0,1})\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}).

For the inductive step, we assume that the statement holds for all words of length k≤nk\leq n. Let u∈𝒲2u\in\mathcal{W}_{2} be a word of length n+1n+1 with exactly one 11, and let ii be the index of the 11. Note that 00 is the only element of 𝒰⁡({0,1})\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}) consisting of all 00’s. Thus, the only way to obtain uu as a concatenation of two previous elements is to concatenate 00 to a word of length nn with exactly one 11. Let vv denote the word of length nn with exactly one 11 at index ii and 00’s everywhere else; let ww denote the word of length nn with exactly one 11 at index i−1i-1 and 00’s everywhere else. We see that u∈𝒰⁡({0,1})u\in\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}) if and only if exactly one of vv and ww is in 𝒰⁡({0,1})\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}). The word vv has binomial coefficient (n−1i−1)\binom{n-1}{i-1} and the word ww has binomial coefficient (n−1i−2)\binom{n-1}{i-2}.

By our inductive hypothesis, uu has a unique representation and is in 𝒰⁡({0,1})\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}) if and only if exactly one of (n−1i−2)\binom{n-1}{i-2} and (n−1i−1)\binom{n-1}{i-1} is odd. Therefore, we must have

(n−1i−2)+(n−1i−1)≡1(mod2).\binom{n-1}{i-2}+\binom{n-1}{i-1}\equiv 1\pmod{2}.

By Pascal’s Identity, (n−1i−2)+(n−1i−1)=(ni−1)\binom{n-1}{i-2}+\binom{n-1}{i-1}=\binom{n}{i-1}, so our equation becomes (ni−1)≡1(mod2)\binom{n}{i-1}\equiv 1\pmod{2}. Note that (ni−1)\binom{n}{i-1} is the binomial coefficient for uu, so u∈𝒰⁡({0,1})u\in\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}) if and only if its binomial coefficient is odd, which completes our induction. ∎

We can now tell if a word with exactly one 11 is in 𝒰⁡({0,1})\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}) by examining the parity of its corresponding binomial coefficient. Note that a word u∈𝒰⁡({0,1})u\in\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}) of length nn with exactly one 11 at index ii has the binomial coefficient (n−1i−1)\binom{n-1}{i-1}, which corresponds to the ii-th number of the (n−1)(n-1)-th row of Pascal’s Triangle.

Gould’s sequence [6] is an integer sequence that counts the number of odd terms in each row of Pascal’s Triangle. Specifically, the nn-th term of Gould’s sequence is the number of odd numbers in the (n−1)(n-1)-th row of Pascal’s Triangle. The first few terms of Gould’s sequence are 1,2,2,4,2,4,4,8,2,4,4,8,4,8,8,161,2,2,4,2,4,4,8,2,4,4,8,4,8,8,16.

Corollary 3.4.

The number of words of length nn in 𝒰⁡({0,1})\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}) with exactly one 11 is the nn-th number in Gould’s sequence.

Theorem 3.3 fully characterizes all words in 𝒰⁡({0,1})\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}) with exactly one 11. We now analyze words in 𝒰⁡({0,1})\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}) with exactly two 11’s.

Theorem 3.5.

Let u∈𝒲2u\in\mathcal{W}_{2} be a word of length n≥2n\geq 2 with exactly two 11’s such that the 11’s are consecutive. The word uu is in 𝒰⁡({0,1})\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}) if and only if nn is odd.

Proof.

We proceed by induction on the length of the word. The base cases are n=2n=2 and n=3n=3. The only word of length 22 with two consecutive 11’s (and the rest 00’s) is 1111; this is not in 𝒰⁡({0,1})\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}). The words of length 33 with two consecutive 11’s (and the rest 00’s) are 011011 and 110110; both are in 𝒰⁡({0,1})\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}) by direct computation.

We now perform the inductive step. Assume that the theorem holds for all words of length strictly smaller than nn. Consider the word uu of length nn which consists of kk 00’s, followed by two 11’s and then ℓ\ell more 00’s, where we must have k≥1k\geq 1 or ℓ≥1\ell\geq 1 since n≥4n\geq 4. By Theorem 3.1, we can assume without loss of generality that k≥1k\geq 1. One representation of uu is the concatenation

u=0⋯0⏟k​11​0⋯0⏟ℓ=0⋯0⏟k​1∗1​0⋯0⏟ℓ,u=\underbrace{0\cdots 0}_{k}11\underbrace{0\cdots 0}_{\ell}=\underbrace{0\cdots 0}_{k}1*1\underbrace{0\cdots 0}_{\ell},

where the elements 0⋯0⏟k​1\underbrace{0\cdots 0}_{k}1 and 1​0⋯0⏟ℓ1\underbrace{0\cdots 0}_{\ell} are in 𝒰⁡({0,1})\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}) by Theorem 3.3. If nn is even, a second representation is given by

u=0⋯0⏟k​11​0⋯0⏟ℓ=0∗0⋯0⏟k−1​11​0⋯0⏟ℓ,u=\underbrace{0\cdots 0}_{k}11\underbrace{0\cdots 0}_{\ell}=0*\underbrace{0\cdots 0}_{k-1}11\underbrace{0\cdots 0}_{\ell},

meaning that uu is not in 𝒰⁡({0,1})\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}). If nn is odd, we claim that there is no second representation. Recall that 00 is the only element of 𝒰⁡({0,1})\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}) consisting of all 00’s, so the only possible second representation of uu would have the form

u=0∗0⋯0⏟k−1​11​0⋯0⏟ℓoru=0⋯0⏟k​11​0⋯0⏟ℓ−1∗0.u=0*\underbrace{0\cdots 0}_{k-1}11\underbrace{0\cdots 0}_{\ell}\quad\text{or}\quad u=\underbrace{0\cdots 0}_{k}11\underbrace{0\cdots 0}_{\ell-1}*0.

But, by the inductive hypothesis, neither 0⋯0⏟k−1​11​0⋯0⏟ℓ\underbrace{0\cdots 0}_{k-1}11\underbrace{0\cdots 0}_{\ell} nor 0⋯0⏟k​11​0⋯0⏟ℓ−1\underbrace{0\cdots 0}_{k}11\underbrace{0\cdots 0}_{\ell-1} is in 𝒰⁡({0,1})\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}), which completes the proof. ∎

Theorem 3.6.

Let u∈𝒲2u\in\mathcal{W}_{2} be a word of length n≥5n\geq 5 with exactly two 11’s such that the 11’s are separated by exactly one 00. The word uu is in 𝒰⁡({0,1})\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}) if and only if nn is even.

Proof.

Again, we proceed by induction on nn. The base cases n=5n=5 and n=6n=6 are easy to check by direct computation.

For the inductive step, assume that the statement holds for all values strictly less than nn. Consider a word uu of length nn consisting of kk 00’s followed by 101101 and then ℓ\ell 00’s. Since n≥5n\geq 5, we must have k≥1k\geq 1 or ℓ≥1\ell\geq 1. By Theorem 3.1, we can assume without loss of generality that k≥1k\geq 1.

Case 11: ℓ=0\ell=0. One representation of uu is the concatenation

u=0⋯0⏟k​101=0⋯0⏟k​1∗01,u=\underbrace{0\cdots 0}_{k}101=\underbrace{0\cdots 0}_{k}1*01,

where 0101 and 0⋯0⏟k​1\underbrace{0\cdots 0}_{k}1 are both elements of 𝒰⁡({0,1})\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}) by Theorem 3.3. If nn is odd, then a second representation of uu as the concatenation of words in 𝒰⁡({0,1})\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}) is given by

u=0⋯0⏟k​101=0⋯0⏟k​10∗1,u=\underbrace{0\cdots 0}_{k}101=\underbrace{0\cdots 0}_{k}10*1,

meaning that uu is not in 𝒰⁡({0,1})\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}). If nn is even, this second representation fails, since 0⋯0⏟k​10\underbrace{0\cdots 0}_{k}10 is not an element of 𝒰⁡({0,1})\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}) by Theorem 3.3. We claim there is no second representation if nn is even. Since 00 is the only element of 𝒰⁡({0,1})\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}), the only other representation of uu would be

u=0∗0⋯0⏟k−1​101.u=0*\underbrace{0\cdots 0}_{k-1}101.

But by the inductive hypothesis, 0⋯0⏟k−1​101\underbrace{0\cdots 0}_{k-1}101 is not in 𝒰⁡({0,1})\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}), so uu must be in 𝒰⁡({0,1})\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}).

Case 2: ℓ≥1\ell\geq 1. If nn is odd, then uu can be represented as

u=0⋯0⏟k​101​0⋯0⏟ℓ=0∗0⋯0⏟k−1​101​0⋯0⏟ℓ=0⋯0⏟k​101​0⋯0⏟ℓ−1∗0,u=\underbrace{0\cdots 0}_{k}101\underbrace{0\cdots 0}_{\ell}=0*\underbrace{0\cdots 0}_{k-1}101\underbrace{0\cdots 0}_{\ell}=\underbrace{0\cdots 0}_{k}101\underbrace{0\cdots 0}_{\ell-1}*0,

where 0⋯0⏟k−1​101​0⋯0⏟ℓ\underbrace{0\cdots 0}_{k-1}101\underbrace{0\cdots 0}_{\ell} and 0⋯0⏟k​101​0⋯0⏟ℓ−1\underbrace{0\cdots 0}_{k}101\underbrace{0\cdots 0}_{\ell-1} are both in 𝒰⁡({0,1})\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}) by our inductive hypothesis. Thus, uu is excluded from 𝒰⁡({0,1})\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}) when nn is odd.

If nn is even, exactly one of 0⋯0⏟k​10\underbrace{0\cdots 0}_{k}10 and 01​0⋯0⏟ℓ01\underbrace{0\cdots 0}_{\ell} will have even length. By Theorem 3.3, exactly one of

u=0⋯0⏟k​101​0⋯0⏟ℓ=0⋯0⏟k​10∗1​0⋯0⏟ℓandu=0⋯0⏟k​1∗01​0⋯0⏟ℓu=\underbrace{0\cdots 0}_{k}101\underbrace{0\cdots 0}_{\ell}=\underbrace{0\cdots 0}_{k}10*1\underbrace{0\cdots 0}_{\ell}\quad\text{and}\quad u=\underbrace{0\cdots 0}_{k}1*01\underbrace{0\cdots 0}_{\ell}

will be a representation of uu as the concatenation of words in 𝒰⁡({0,1})\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}).

Since 00 is the only word in 𝒰⁡({0,1})\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}) that consists entirely of 00’s, the remaining two possible representations of uu are

u=0⋯0⏟k​101​0⋯0⏟ℓ=0∗0⋯0⏟k−1​101​0⋯0⏟ℓandu=0⋯0⏟k​101​0⋯0⏟ℓ−1∗0.u=\underbrace{0\cdots 0}_{k}101\underbrace{0\cdots 0}_{\ell}=0*\underbrace{0\cdots 0}_{k-1}101\underbrace{0\cdots 0}_{\ell}\quad\text{and}\quad u=\underbrace{0\cdots 0}_{k}101\underbrace{0\cdots 0}_{\ell-1}*0.

But by our inductive hypothesis, neither 0⋯0⏟k−1​101​0⋯0⏟ℓ\underbrace{0\cdots 0}_{k-1}101\underbrace{0\cdots 0}_{\ell} nor 0⋯0⏟k​101​0⋯0⏟ℓ−1\underbrace{0\cdots 0}_{k}101\underbrace{0\cdots 0}_{\ell-1} is in 𝒰⁡({0,1}),\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}), which means uu is in 𝒰⁡({0,1})\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}) if nn is even. ∎

While Theorem 3.5 and Theorem 3.6 characterize an infinite set of words with exactly two 11’s in 𝒰⁡({0,1})\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}) satisfying specific conditions, they do not apply to all words with exactly two 11’s. We now give a general necessary condition for a word with two 11’s to be in 𝒰⁡({0,1})\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}).

Theorem 3.7.

Let u∈𝒲2u\in\mathcal{W}_{2} be a word of length n≥2n\geq 2 with exactly two 11’s, and let i1<i2i_{1}<i_{2} be the indices of the two 11’s. If uu is in 𝒰⁡({0,1})\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}), then

i2−i1≤n2.i_{2}-i_{1}\leq\frac{n}{2}.

We first require a preparatory lemma. For nonnegative integers aa, bb, and nn, let

Sa,b,n={i:(ia)​(n−ib)≡1(mod2)}.S_{a,b,n}=\left\{i:\binom{i}{a}\binom{n-i}{b}\equiv 1\pmod{2}\right\}.

Sa,b,nS_{a,b,n} roughly counts the ways in which a string of length n+2n+2 with two 11’s at the indices a+1a+1 and n+2−bn+2-b can be formed as the concatenation of two strings in 𝒰⁡({0,1})\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}), each containing one 11. Thus, we must understand Sa,b,nS_{a,b,n} because it yields insight into different representations of words in 𝒲2\mathcal{W}_{2} with exactly two 11’s.

Lemma 3.8.

For all nonnegative integers a,b,na,b,n such that a+b<n2,a+b<\frac{n}{2}, we have |Sa,b,n|≠1.|S_{a,b,n}|\neq 1.

Proof.

Assume that |Sa,b,n|≥1|S_{a,b,n}|\geq 1, so that there is some i∈Sa,b,ni\in S_{a,b,n}. We have

(ia)​(n−ib)≡1(mod2).\binom{i}{a}\binom{n-i}{b}\equiv 1\pmod{2}.

Given i∈Sa,b,ni\in S_{a,b,n}, we aim to exhibit a second element i′∈Sa,b,ni^{\prime}\in S_{a,b,n}.

Consider the binary representations a=ak​2k+ak−1​2k−1+⋯+a1​2+a0=akak−1⋯a1a0¯a=a_{k}2^{k}+a_{k-1}2^{k-1}+\cdots+a_{1}2+a_{0}=\overline{a_{k}a_{k-1}\cdots a_{1}a_{0}}, b=bkbk−1⋯b1b0¯b=\overline{b_{k}b_{k-1}\cdots b_{1}b_{0}}, i=ikik−1⋯i1i0¯i=\overline{i_{k}i_{k-1}\cdots i_{1}i_{0}}, and n−i=(n−i)k(n−i)k−1⋯(n−i)1(n−i)0¯n-i=\overline{(n-i)_{k}(n-i)_{k-1}\cdots(n-i)_{1}(n-i)_{0}}, where kk is sufficiently large so that aa, bb, ii, and n−in-i all have leading 00’s. Let jj with 0≤j≤k0\leq j\leq k be the maximum value such that aj=bj=0a_{j}=b_{j}=0 but at least one of ij=1i_{j}=1 or (n−i)j=1(n-i)_{j}=1; such a jj exists since a+b<n2a+b<\frac{n}{2}. If exactly one of iji_{j} and (n−i)j(n-i)_{j} equals 11, then assume without loss of generality that ij=1i_{j}=1 and (n−i)j=0(n-i)_{j}=0. This loses no generality because we can swap aa with bb and ii with n−in-i. By Lucas’ Theorem [11], the choice i′=i−2ji^{\prime}=i-2^{j} and n−i′=(n−i)+2jn-i^{\prime}=(n-i)+2^{j} satisfies

(i′a)​(n−i′b)≡1(mod2).\binom{i^{\prime}}{a}\binom{n-i^{\prime}}{b}\equiv 1\pmod{2}.

On the other hand, if ij=(n−i)j=1i_{j}=(n-i)_{j}=1, then let mm with k≥m>jk\geq m>j be the smallest value such that im=0i_{m}=0 or (n−i)m=0(n-i)_{m}=0. Without loss of generality, assume that im=0i_{m}=0.

For m>x>jm>x>j, at least one of ax=0a_{x}=0 or bx=0b_{x}=0; otherwise, the maximum possible value of nn would be 2​(a−2x)+2​(b−2x)+2​(1+2+⋯+2x−1+2x)2(a-2^{x})+2(b-2^{x})+2(1+2+\cdots+2^{x-1}+2^{x}), since jj is the largest index where aj=bj=0a_{j}=b_{j}=0 but ij=1i_{j}=1 or (n−i)j=1(n-i)_{j}=1. But then n2≤a−2x+b+1+2+⋯+2x−1<a+b\frac{n}{2}\leq a-2^{x}+b+1+2+\cdots+2^{x-1}<a+b. Thus, if ax=1a_{x}=1, then bx=0b_{x}=0. Furthermore, mm is defined such that ix=(n−i)x=1i_{x}=(n-i)_{x}=1 for all m>x>jm>x>j.

By Lucas’ Theorem [11],

i′=i−2j−(∑j<x<m,ax=02x)+2mi^{\prime}=i-2^{j}-\left(\sum_{j<x<m,a_{x}=0}2^{x}\right)+2^{m}

with

n−i′=(n−i)−2j−(∑j<x<m,ax=12x)n-i^{\prime}=(n-i)-2^{j}-\left(\sum_{j<x<m,a_{x}=1}2^{x}\right)

therefore also satisfies

(i′a)​(n−i′b)≡1(mod2),\binom{i^{\prime}}{a}\binom{n-i^{\prime}}{b}\equiv 1\pmod{2},

which implies that |Sa,b,n|≠1|S_{a,b,n}|\neq 1. ∎

Now we are ready to prove Theorem 3.7.

Proof of Theorem 3.7.

For any word uu of length nn with exactly two 11’s, at indices i1i_{1} and i2i_{2}, that satisfies i2−i1>n2i_{2}-i_{1}>\frac{n}{2}, we wish to prove uu is not in 𝒰⁡({0,1})\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}).

In particular, we wish to prove that uu can be constructed as the concatenation of two smaller words in 𝒰⁡({0,1})\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}) in either zero or at least two ways. We consider the possible representations of uu as a concatenation of two previous elements, u1u_{1} and u2u_{2}, of 𝒰⁡({0,1})\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}). First, we rule out the case where one of u1u_{1} and u2u_{2} contains both 11’s, by induction on nn. Thus, we restrict our attention to expressions of u=u1∗u2u=u_{1}*u_{2} as the concatenation of two smaller words u1u_{1} and u2u_{2} in 𝒰⁡({0,1})\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}), each with exactly one 11.

We note that the index of the 11 in u1u_{1} is i1i_{1}, while the index of the 11, from right to left, in u2u_{2} is n−i2+1n-i_{2}+1. By Theorem 3.3, we therefore wish to prove that if kk is the length of u1u_{1} (so that u2u_{2} has length n−kn-k), then there exists either 00 or at least 22 possible values of kk such that

(k−1i1−1)≡1(mod2)and((n−2)−(k−1)n−i2)≡1(mod2).\binom{k-1}{i_{1}-1}\equiv 1\pmod{2}\quad\text{and}\quad\binom{(n-2)-(k-1)}{n-i_{2}}\equiv 1\pmod{2}.

Note that since i2−i1>n2i_{2}-i_{1}>\frac{n}{2}, (i1−1)+(n−i2)<n−22(i_{1}-1)+(n-i_{2})<\frac{n-2}{2}. We therefore see that the number of ways to express uu as the concatenation of two words in 𝒰⁡({0,1})\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}), each consisting of one 11, is |Si1−1,n−i2,n−2||S_{i_{1}-1,n-i_{2},n-2}|. By Lemma 3.8, however, |Si1−1,n−i2,n−2|≠1|S_{i_{1}-1,n-i_{2},n-2}|\neq 1; hence, all such uu with i2−i1>n2i_{2}-i_{1}>\frac{n}{2} are excluded from 𝒰⁡({0,1})\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}). ∎

We note that i2−i1≤n2i_{2}-i_{1}\leq\frac{n}{2} is a tight bound and that Lemma 3.8 no longer holds when a+b=n2a+b=\frac{n}{2}. In particular, 001001001001, 000001000001000001000001, 000010000010000010000010, and 0000100000010000001000000100 are all examples of words in 𝒰⁡({0,1})\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}) that satisfy i2−i1=n2i_{2}-i_{1}=\frac{n}{2}.

3.3. The column phenomenon

Kravitz and Steinerberger observed a column phenomenon in Ulam sets of certain commutative settings [9]. We extend this notion to the noncommutative setting of free groups and prove a similar result for 𝒰⁡({0,1})\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}).

They proved that in certain commutative Ulam sets in ℤ2\mathbb{Z}^{2}, all the columns (each obtained by fixing a xx-coordinate) are eventually periodic. This does not readily apply to 𝒰⁡({0,1})\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}); instead, we extend this notion of columns by fixing a suitable infinitely long word and considering all its prefixes.

More precisely, for a word t∈𝒲2t\in\mathcal{W}_{2} of length mm, define T=t∗t∗t∗⋯T=t*t*t*\cdots to be the infinitely long word consisting of the concatenation of infinitely many copies of tt.

For 0≤i<m0\leq i<m, denote by Ti,jT_{i,j} the subword of TT consisting of the jj consecutive letters in TT starting after the ii-th index. For simplicity, let TkT_{k} be another expression for T0,kT_{0,k}.

Theorem 3.9.

If for any 0≤i<m0\leq i<m, the set of values kk for which Ti,kT_{i,k} is in 𝒰⁡({0,1})\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}) is eventually periodic, then for all words u∈𝒲2u\in\mathcal{W}_{2}, the set of values kk for which u∗Tku*T_{k} is in 𝒰⁡({0,1})\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}) is also eventually periodic.

Proof.

We proceed by induction on the length, nn, of word uu. For the base case, n=0n=0, we already assumed that the values kk for which TkT_{k} is in 𝒰⁡({0,1})\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}) are eventually periodic.

For the inductive step, assume that the theorem holds for all words of length less than nn. Then for a word uu of length nn, there are two potential ways to represent u∗Tku*T_{k} as the product of two smaller terms in 𝒰⁡({0,1})\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}):

  1. (1)

    u∗Tk=u1∗(u2∗Tk)u*T_{k}=u_{1}*(u_{2}*T_{k}), where u1∗u2=uu_{1}*u_{2}=u and u1u_{1} and u2u_{2} are words of positive length.

  2. (2)

    u∗Tk=(u∗Tk−k′)∗Ti,k′u*T_{k}=(u*T_{k-k^{\prime}})*T_{i,k^{\prime}}, where i≡k−k′(modm)i\equiv k-k^{\prime}\pmod{m}, 0≤i<m0\leq i<m, and we consider u∗T0u*T_{0} to be equal to uu.

Let’s first disregard the second case. Note that there are n−1n-1 ways to represent uu as u1∗u2u_{1}*u_{2}, as necessary for the first case. By our inductive hypothesis, the set of values kk such that u2∗Tku_{2}*T_{k} is in 𝒰⁡({0,1})\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}) is eventually periodic for all n−1n-1 such u2u_{2}. Thus, if PP is the least common multiple of their periods, there exists some large KK such that, for any u2u_{2} and for k>Kk>K, u2∗Tk∈𝒰⁡({0,1})u_{2}*T_{k}\in\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}) if and only if u2∗Tk+P∈𝒰⁡({0,1})u_{2}*T_{k+P}\in\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}). Note that the number of representations of u∗Tku*T_{k} as u1∗(u2∗Tk)u_{1}*(u_{2}*T_{k}) depends solely on whether each u2∗Tku_{2}*T_{k} is in 𝒰⁡({0,1})\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}), since each u1u_{1} is fixed. But for k>Kk>K, u2∗Tku_{2}*T_{k} is in 𝒰⁡({0,1})\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}) if and only if u2∗Tk+Pu_{2}*T_{k+P} is included. Thus, if we define

bu,k={0if there are no such representations of u∗Tk1if there is exactly one such representation of u∗Tk2+otherwise,b_{u,k}=\begin{cases}0&\text{if there are no such representations of $u*T_{k}$}\\ 1&\text{if there is exactly one such representation of $u*T_{k}$}\\ 2_{+}&\text{otherwise}\end{cases},

then (bu,k)(b_{u,k}) is eventually periodic in kk with period PP.

Now, we account for the second case. We will show that the periodicity still holds (though the period can change) when also considering representations of the form u∗Tk=(u∗Tk−k′)∗T0,k′u*T_{k}=(u*T_{k-k^{\prime}})*T_{0,k^{\prime}} (when i=0i=0 and so k≡k′≡0(modm)k\equiv k^{\prime}\equiv 0\pmod{m}). We assumed that the values k′k^{\prime} such that Tk′T_{k^{\prime}} is in 𝒰⁡({0,1})\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}) are eventually periodic. We can therefore split up the values k′k^{\prime} for which Tk′T_{k^{\prime}} is in 𝒰⁡({0,1})\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}) into a finite non-periodic transient phase and a periodic phase.

Similar to (bu,k)(b_{u,k}), let (cu,k)(c_{u,k}) denote the number of representations of u∗Tku*T_{k} where we now also consider possible representations u∗Tk=(u∗Tk−k′)∗T0,k′u*T_{k}=(u*T_{k-k^{\prime}})*T_{0,k^{\prime}} where k′k^{\prime} is in the periodic phase. For simplicity, we similarly let cu,kc_{u,k} to be equal to 2+2_{+} if it has at least 22 such representations.

For a fixed equivalence class, RR, modulo P​P0PP_{0}, consider all equivalence classes R−SR-S, where S∈CS\in C. Then any k−k′≡0(modm)k-k^{\prime}\equiv 0\pmod{m} in any of the equivalence classes R−SR-S such that u∗Tk−k′∈𝒰⁡({0,1})u*T_{k-k^{\prime}}\in\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}) yields a representation of u∗Tku*T_{k} for sufficiently large k∈Rk\in R. Thus, if there are two or more such elements, cu,k=2+c_{u,k}=2_{+} for sufficiently large k∈Rk\in R. If there is one such element, then cu,k=bu,k+1c_{u,k}=b_{u,k}+1, and if there is no such element then cu,k=bu,kc_{u,k}=b_{u,k}, for sufficiently large k∈Rk\in R. Thus, the sequence (cu,k)(c_{u,k}) is still eventually periodic, though with period P​P0PP_{0}.

Similar to (cu,k)(c_{u,k}), let (cu,k′)(c^{\prime}_{u,k}) denote the number of representations of u∗Tku*T_{k} where we now also account for all of the representations u∗Tk=(u∗Tk−k′)∗Ti,k′u*T_{k}=(u*T_{k-k^{\prime}})*T_{i,k^{\prime}} where k′k^{\prime} is in the periodic phase of Ti,xT_{i,x}. The same argument above of the periodic case for i=0i=0 can similarly be repeatedly applied and extended to the other m−1m-1 periodic phases, corresponding to i=1,…,m−1i=1,\ldots,m-1, to show that (cu,k′)(c^{\prime}_{u,k}) is also periodic.

Now, all that’s left is for us to account for the mm finite transient phases. Whether u∗Tku*T_{k} is now included depends solely on cu,k′c^{\prime}_{u,k}, and for each word Ti,x∈𝒰⁡({0,1})T_{i,x}\in\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}) from one of the transient phases with i+x≡k(modm)i+x\equiv k\pmod{m}, whether u∗Tk−xu*T_{k-x} is in 𝒰⁡({0,1})\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}). This is a recurrence relation describing whether u∗Tku*T_{k} is in 𝒰⁡({0,1})\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}) in terms of which of the u∗Tk−xu*T_{k-x} are included. However, there are only finitely many such elements Ti,xT_{i,x}, and cu,k′c^{\prime}_{u,k} is periodic for large enough kk, so this recurrence relation has finitely many states. Hence, it must also be eventually periodic.

We therefore conclude, after fully considering all possibilities, that the values kk for which u∗Tku*T_{k} is in 𝒰⁡({0,1})\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}) are eventually periodic. ∎

For the special case when t=0t=0 and T=000⋯T=000\cdots is simply an infinitely long word of all 00’s, Theorem 3.9 implies that adding arbitrarily number of 00’s to the end of a word uu will always create new words that are eventually periodically included in 𝒰⁡({0,1})\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}). Indeed, we note that Theorems 3.5 and 3.6 are special cases of this property for u=0⋯0⏟n​11u=\underbrace{0\cdots 0}_{n}11 and 0⋯0⏟n​101\underbrace{0\cdots 0}_{n}101, respectively (where nn is some nonnegative integer).

We also see, by Lucas’ Theorem [11], that Theorem 3.3 shows the existence of this special case of the column phenomenon for words with exactly one 11 since the binomial coefficients are eventually periodic modulo 22.

3.4. Density

We now consider the density of the Ulam set 𝒰⁡({0,1})\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}) in the following sense. Let 𝒲2,n\mathcal{W}_{2,n} denote the set of all binary words of length nn, and let Vn=𝒰⁡({0,1})∩𝒲2,nV_{n}=\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\})\cap\mathcal{W}_{2,n}. We are interested in the quantity |Vn|/|𝒲2,n||V_{n}|/|\mathcal{W}_{2,n}|, which represents the density of the Ulam set among all binary words of length nn.

Here are the plotted values of |Vn|/|𝒲2,n||V_{n}|/|\mathcal{W}_{2,n}| for n<25n<25, obtained from a computer-generated list of all 69003446900344 words in 𝒰⁡({0,1})\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}) of length less than 2525.

We notice that densities |Vn|/|𝒲2,n||V_{n}|/|\mathcal{W}_{2,n}| seem to converge at some real value rr. In particular, we compute

|V24|/|𝒲2,24|=3406884224=8517214194304≈0.20306611.|V_{24}|/|\mathcal{W}_{2,24}|=\frac{3406884}{2^{24}}=\frac{851721}{4194304}\approx 0.20306611.
Conjecture 3.10.

There exists some 0<r<10<r<1 such that the density of the Ulam set 𝒰⁡({0,1})\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}) is asymptotically equal to rr. More formally, we have

limn→∞|Vn||𝒲2,n|=limn→∞|Vn|2n=r.\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{|V_{n}|}{|\mathcal{W}_{2,n}|}=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{|V_{n}|}{2^{n}}=r.

Note that Conjecture 3.10 is analogous to the problem of finding the density of the classical Ulam sequence, which empirical calculations suggest is approximately 0.0740.074 [5].

3.5. 𝒱\mathcal{V}-sets in free groups

While 𝒰⁡({0,1})\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}) contains periodic and structured properties, a lot is still unknown about its behavior. However, 𝒱⁡({0,1})\mathcal{V}(\{0,1\}), the variant of the Ulam set 𝒰⁡({0,1})\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}) that allows words to be concatenated with themselves, can be fully characterized.

Theorem 3.11.

A word uu of length nn is in 𝒱⁡({0,1})\mathcal{V}(\{0,1\}) if and only if nn is a power of 22.

Proof.

We induct on nn. For the base case, n=1n=1, we see that both 00 and 11 are included in 𝒱⁡({0,1})\mathcal{V}(\{0,1\}).

For the inductive step, assume the theorem holds for all words of length less than nn. Then for a word uu of length nn, denote by ui,ju_{i,j} the subword of uu consisting of the jj consecutive letters in uu starting after the ii-th index. If n=2k+1n=2^{k+1} is a power of 22, then by the inductive hypothesis, all words of length 2k2^{k} are in 𝒱⁡({0,1})\mathcal{V}(\{0,1\}), but no words of length strictly between 2k2^{k} and 2k+12^{k+1} are included. Thus, uu has a unique representation as the concatenation of smaller words in 𝒱⁡({0,1})\mathcal{V}(\{0,1\}),

u=u0,2k∗u2k,2k,u=u_{0,2^{k}}*u_{2^{k},2^{k}},

consisting of concatenating the first half of uu with the second half. Therefore, uu is included in the 𝒱\mathcal{V}-set.

If nn is not a power of 22 and cannot be written as the sum of two powers of 22, then uu cannot be represented as the concatenation of smaller words in 𝒱⁡({0,1})\mathcal{V}(\{0,1\}) by our inductive hypothesis. Otherwise, if n=2i+2jn=2^{i}+2^{j} is not a power of 22, and so i≠ji\neq j, but can be written as the sum of two powers of 22, then by the inductive hypothesis,

u=u0,2i∗u2i,2j=u0,2j∗u2j,2iu=u_{0,2^{i}}*u_{2^{i},2^{j}}=u_{0,2^{j}}*u_{2^{j},2^{i}}

are two different representations of uu as the concatenation of smaller terms in 𝒱⁡({0,1})\mathcal{V}(\{0,1\}). Thus, uu is excluded in this case. ∎

4. Ulam sets in ℤ×(ℤ/n​ℤ)\mathbb{Z}\times(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})

We now focus solely on Ulam sets in commutative settings. Suppose we have an abelian group GG and a finite initial set S⊂GS\subset G. In [9], Kravitz and Steinerberger proved that the choice of the notion of size that determines the order in which the elements are added to 𝒰⁡(S)\mathcal{U}(S) does not actually affect the set itself. Thus, only the initial set SS is needed to construct 𝒰⁡(S)\mathcal{U}(S). Moreover, it is easy to see that there exists a suitable size function for an initial set S={v1,…,vk}S=\{v_{1},\ldots,v_{k}\} (in the sense of Theorem 2 from [9]) if and only if the equation

a1​v1+…+ak​vk=0a_{1}v_{1}+\ldots+a_{k}v_{k}=0

has no solution (a1,…,ak)(a_{1},\ldots,a_{k}) in nonnegative integers where not all a1,…,aka_{1},\ldots,a_{k} are zero.

If we allow negative integers, however, then this equation can have nontrivial solutions in general. Kravitz and Steinerberger also proved in [9] that the structure of the Ulam set depends only on the solutions to this equation, called the characteristic equation of the Ulam set. More precisely, we define two Ulam sets 𝒰1=𝒰⁡({v1,…,vk})\mathcal{U}_{1}=\mathcal{U}(\{v_{1},\ldots,v_{k}\}) and 𝒰2=𝒰⁡({w1,…,wk})\mathcal{U}_{2}=\mathcal{U}(\{w_{1},\ldots,w_{k}\}) to be structurally equivalent if, for all (a1,…,ak)∈ℤk(a_{1},\ldots,a_{k})\in\mathbb{Z}^{k},

a1​v1+⋯+ak​vk∈𝒰1⟺a1​w1+⋯+ak​wk∈𝒰2a_{1}v_{1}+\cdots+a_{k}v_{k}\in\mathcal{U}_{1}\Longleftrightarrow a_{1}w_{1}+\cdots+a_{k}w_{k}\in\mathcal{U}_{2}

(note that this is related to the idea of Freiman homomorphisms). They proved that two Ulam sets with the same set of solutions of their characteristic equation are structurally equivalent. Note that if we let LL be the set of solutions to the characteristic equation, then LL must form a subgroup of ℤk\mathbb{Z}^{k}. We will therefore call LL the associated lattice of the Ulam set. Because of this structural equivalence, we will often refer to the Ulam set with associated lattice LL since all Ulam sets with associated lattice LL are structurally equivalent.

The condition on the generators implies that L∩ℤ≥0k={0}L\cap\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{k}=\{0\}. Furthermore, we cannot have a vector of the form ei−eje_{i}-e_{j} with i≠ji\neq j in LL (where eke_{k} is the canonical basis vector with a 11 in the kk-th position and 00’s everywhere else), since it would imply that vi=vjv_{i}=v_{j}. Conversely, for any lattice satisfying those two conditions, we can find an Ulam set having LL as its associated lattice: take GG to be the quotient group ℤk/L\mathbb{Z}^{k}/L and v1,…,vkv_{1},\ldots,v_{k} to be the images of the canonical basis vectors of ℤk\mathbb{Z}^{k} in this quotient. Thus, there is a one-to-one correspondence (up to structural equivalence) between Ulam sets over commutative groups with kk generators and lattices in ℤk\mathbb{Z}^{k} not intersecting ℤ≥0k∖{0}\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{k}\setminus\{0\} that contains no vector ei−eje_{i}-e_{j} for i≠ji\neq j. A particular Ulam set in a particular setting with given associated lattice LL is called an embedding.

The case of two generators is particularly interesting: LL clearly cannot be two-dimensional, so it must either be one-dimensional or be the zero lattice (which corresponds to the simple case of two linearly independent generators, treated in [9]). Thus, all the nontrivial cases correspond to one-dimensional lattices in ℤ2\mathbb{Z}^{2}, which are characterized by a generator (−a,b)(-a,b) where a,b>0a,b>0 and a,ba,b are not both 11. In particular, the classical Ulam sequence in ℤ\mathbb{Z} with initial set {1,2}\{1,2\} corresponds to the lattice generated by (−2,1)(-2,1).

If aa and bb are relatively prime, we can find an embedding in ℤ\mathbb{Z} by taking v1=bv_{1}=b and v2=av_{2}=a. The interesting new cases appear when d=gcd⁡(a,b)>1d=\gcd(a,b)>1; in this case, there is clearly no embedding in ℤm\mathbb{Z}^{m}, since if we have v1,v2∈ℤmv_{1},v_{2}\in\mathbb{Z}^{m} such that −a​v1+b​v2=0-av_{1}+bv_{2}=0, then we also have −ad​v1+bd​v2=0-\frac{a}{d}v_{1}+\frac{b}{d}v_{2}=0. It can, however, be embedded in ℤ×(ℤ/d​ℤ)\mathbb{Z}\times(\mathbb{Z}/d\mathbb{Z}). Indeed, let a′=a/da^{\prime}=a/d, b′=b/db^{\prime}=b/d and choose u,vu,v such that u​a′−b​v′=1ua^{\prime}-bv^{\prime}=1. Then we can take v1=(b′,u)v_{1}=(b^{\prime},u) and v2=(a′,v)v_{2}=(a^{\prime},v), and it is straightforward to check that the corresponding Ulam set has associated lattice generated by (−a,b)(-a,b).

Because of this universality, we study, in this section, Ulam sets in ℤ×(ℤ/n​ℤ)\mathbb{Z}\times(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}). Note that exploring this setting also originates naturally from complex multiplication. Indeed, as noted in [9], Ulam sets arising from multiplication in ℝ\mathbb{R} are equivalent to those arising from addition via a logarithm. But in ℂ\mathbb{C}, the logarithm maps us to ℝ×𝕋\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{T} (under addition), which suggests the investigation of the discrete analog ℤ×(ℤ/n​ℤ)\mathbb{Z}\times(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}).

In this particular setting, the condition that the characteristic equation has no nontrivial solution in nonnegative integers corresponds to the condition that all the initial elements (x,y)∈ℤ×(ℤ/n​ℤ)(x,y)\in\mathbb{Z}\times(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}) must have positive xx-coordinate (or all negative in which case we can negate all terms). We will discuss the regularity of these Ulam sets, decomposition of elements in terms of the initial generators, and the possibility of them being finite.

4.1. Regular Ulam sets

In this section, we analyze the regularity of Ulam sets. This phenomenon has been studied extensively in the past for Ulam sequences and sets in ℤd\mathbb{Z}^{d} [2, 3, 9, 14], but not in ℤ×(ℤ/n​ℤ)\mathbb{Z}\times(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}).

Definition 4.1.

We say that a set 𝒮⊂ℤ≥0×(ℤ/n​ℤ)\mathcal{S}\subset\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}\times(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}) is regular if there exists some period P>0P>0 such that, for sufficiently large xx, we have (x,y)∈𝒮(x,y)\in\mathcal{S} if and only if (x+P,y)∈𝒮(x+P,y)\in\mathcal{S}.

This is an extension of the notion of regularity of a sequence in ℤ\mathbb{Z}, which corresponds to the case n=1n=1 since ℤ\mathbb{Z} is equivalent to ℤ×(ℤ/1​ℤ)\mathbb{Z}\times(\mathbb{Z}/1\mathbb{Z}). In this particular setting, Finch [3] proved that an Ulam sequence with finitely many even terms must be regular. In the same paper, he also conjectured that all regular Ulam sequences in ℤ\mathbb{Z} satisfy this condition. In ℤ×(ℤ/n​ℤ)\mathbb{Z}\times(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}), the situation is more complicated, but the following theorem gives a useful characterization of regular Ulam sets similar to Finch’s result.

Theorem 4.2.

An Ulam set 𝒰\mathcal{U} in ℤ×(ℤ/n​ℤ)\mathbb{Z}\times(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}) is regular if and only if there exists some regular subset E⊂ℤ×(ℤ/n​ℤ)E\subset\mathbb{Z}\times(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}) such that the sum of two elements of EE is never in EE and only finitely many elements of 𝒰\mathcal{U} are not in EE.

Proof.

We start by showing that the existence of such an EE guarantees the regularity of 𝒰\mathcal{U}. Let MM be the greatest xx-coordinate of all elements of 𝒰∖E\mathcal{U}\setminus E, and let PP be the period of EE. For any xx, let Ex={y∈ℤ/n​ℤ:(x,y)∈E}E_{x}=\{y\in\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}:(x,y)\in E\} and 𝒰x={y∈ℤ/n​ℤ:(x,y)∈𝒰}\mathcal{U}_{x}=\{y\in\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}:(x,y)\in\mathcal{U}\}.

For each xx, consider the MM-tuple Lx=(𝒰x−1,𝒰x−2,…,𝒰x−M)L_{x}=(\mathcal{U}_{x-1},\mathcal{U}_{x-2},\ldots,\mathcal{U}_{x-M}). Since there are only 2M​n2^{Mn} possible such tuples, there is some x0>Mx_{0}>M and k>0k>0 such that Lx0=Lx0+k​PL_{x_{0}}=L_{x_{0}+kP}. By taking x0x_{0} to be sufficiently large, we know, by the regularity of EE, that Ex=Ex+k​PE_{x}=E_{x+kP} for every x≥x0x\geq x_{0}. It then suffices to show for x≥x0x\geq x_{0} that ExE_{x} and LxL_{x} together uniquely determine 𝒰x\mathcal{U}_{x}, since applying it to x0,x0+1,x0+2,…x_{0},x_{0}+1,x_{0}+2,\ldots will prove that 𝒰\mathcal{U} is regular.

However, we see that this is a consequence of the condition that the sum of two elements of EE is never in EE. In particular, if y∈Exy\in E_{x}, then any representation of (x,y)(x,y) as a sum of previous elements of 𝒰\mathcal{U} must use one of the finitely many elements from 𝒰∖E\mathcal{U}\setminus E. Thus, (x,y)(x,y) is in 𝒰\mathcal{U} if and only if exactly one of (x,y)−p(x,y)-p is in 𝒰\mathcal{U} for p∈𝒰∖Ep\in\mathcal{U}\setminus E. Moreover, if y∉Exy\not\in E_{x} then (x,y)∉𝒰(x,y)\not\in\mathcal{U} because x≥x0>Mx\geq x_{0}>M. This is enough to show that ExE_{x} and LxL_{x} together uniquely determine 𝒰x\mathcal{U}_{x}.

Now, for the converse, we only need to show that there exists such an EE given that 𝒰\mathcal{U} is regular with period PP. It suffices to take EE to be the periodic section of 𝒰\mathcal{U}. We see that, with this construction, EE is regular and that only finitely many elements of 𝒰\mathcal{U} are not in it. Now suppose that (x1,y1)(x_{1},y_{1}) and (x2,y2)(x_{2},y_{2}) are both in EE, with x1≤x2x_{1}\leq x_{2}. Then, since EE is the periodic section, we have the two distinct representations

(x1+x2+3​P,y1+y2)=(x1,y1)+(x2+3​P,y2)=(x1+P,y1)+(x2+2​P,y2),(x_{1}+x_{2}+3P,y_{1}+y_{2})=(x_{1},y_{1})+(x_{2}+3P,y_{2})=(x_{1}+P,y_{1})+(x_{2}+2P,y_{2}),

so (x1+x2+3​P,y1+y2)∉𝒰(x_{1}+x_{2}+3P,y_{1}+y_{2})\not\in\mathcal{U} and (x1+x2,y1+y2)∉𝒰(x_{1}+x_{2},y_{1}+y_{2})\not\in\mathcal{U}. This satisfies all the properties of EE, so the proof is complete. ∎

Note that, when n=1n=1, the backwards direction of Theorem 4.2 recovers a known result of Ross (the first part of Theorem 6.3.2 from [13]). Finch’s result [3] is also a consequence of Theorem 4.2 for the case n=1n=1 when EE is the set of odd numbers. More generally, we have the following:

Corollary 4.3.

Let 𝒰\mathcal{U} be an Ulam set in ℤ×(ℤ/n​ℤ)\mathbb{Z}\times(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}) with two generators, v1v_{1} and v2v_{2}, and associated lattice generated by (−a,b)(-a,b). Then the following must be true:

  1. (1)

    If 𝒰\mathcal{U} contains finitely many elements with an even xx-coordinate, it is regular.

  2. (2)

    If nn is even and 𝒰\mathcal{U} contains finitely many elements with an even yy-coordinate, it is regular.

  3. (3)

    If aa is even and 𝒰\mathcal{U} contains finitely many elements of the form 2​x​v1+y​v22xv_{1}+yv_{2}, it is regular.

Proof.

Take EE, in Theorem 4.2, to be

  1. (1)

    the set of elements with an odd xx-coordinate.

  2. (2)

    the set of elements with an odd yy-coordinate.

  3. (3)

    the set of elements of the form x​v1+y​v2xv_{1}+yv_{2}, where xx is odd.

It is straightforward to check that these choices of EE satisfy the conditions of Theorem 4.2, so 𝒰\mathcal{U} must be regular. ∎

These choices of EE, especially the third one, seem to readily apply for most regular Ulam sets that we have encountered. More precisely, computations have shown that the following conjecture seems to hold:

Conjecture 4.4.

Let a>2a>2 be even and bb be sufficiently large. An Ulam set with generators v1v_{1} and v2v_{2} and associated lattice generated by (−a,b)(-a,b) contains finitely many elements of the form 2​x​v1+y​v22xv_{1}+yv_{2} and is therefore regular.

This is in agreement with Finch’s conjecture [3] about exactly which sequences in ℤ\mathbb{Z} are regular (corresponding to the case where aa and bb are relatively prime). The main difficulty behind proving Conjecture 4.4 is that when aa becomes large, there can be many elements outside of EE (of the form 2​x​v1+y​v22xv_{1}+yv_{2}), making it hard to characterize the elements of 𝒰\mathcal{U}.

We now focus on the case a=2a=2. Note that this case is not included in Conjecture 4.4 because when bb is a power of two, there are infinitely many elements of the form 2​x​v1+y​v22xv_{1}+yv_{2}. For all other values of bb, however, there are only two such elements. This generalizes Schmerl and Spiegel’s theorem [14] that states that an Ulam sequence in ℤ\mathbb{Z} generated by a=2a=2 and b>3b>3, where b is odd, has exactly two even terms. Our result allows bb to be even (in which case the Ulam set cannot be embedded in ℤ\mathbb{Z}).

Theorem 4.5.

Let b>3b>3, and let 𝒰\mathcal{U} be an Ulam set generated by two elements v1v_{1} and v2v_{2} with associated lattice generated by (−2,b)(-2,b). If bb is not a power of 22, then 𝒰\mathcal{U} contains exactly two terms of the form 2​x​v1+y​v22xv_{1}+yv_{2}: v2v_{2} and (b+1)​v2=2​v1+v2(b+1)v_{2}=2v_{1}+v_{2}.

The beginning of our proof is largely based off of the original proof where bb is odd. We will need to compute the first few elements of 𝒰\mathcal{U}. Note that, by adding a suitable multiple of −2​v1+b​v2-2v_{1}+bv_{2}, each element of 𝒰\mathcal{U} can be expressed uniquely as x​v1+y​v2x{v_{1}}+y{v_{2}} for x∈{0,1}x\in\{0,1\} and y≥0y\geq 0.

Lemma 4.6.

The elements of 𝒰\mathcal{U} of the form v1+y​v2v_{1}+yv_{2} for 0≤y≤3​b+20\leq y\leq 3b+2 are those with exactly one of the following:

  1. (1)

    0≤y≤b0\leq y\leq b,

  2. (2)

    b<y≤2​bb<y\leq 2b, where y≡b(mod2)y\equiv b\pmod{2},

  3. (3)

    2​b<y≤3​b+22b<y\leq 3b+2, where y≡−1,0(mod4)y\equiv-1,0\pmod{4}.

Furthermore, the elements of 𝒰\mathcal{U} of the form y​v2yv_{2} for 0≤y≤3​b+20\leq y\leq 3b+2 are those with y=1y=1 or y=b+1y=b+1.

Proof.

This is straightforward with strong induction on yy, and where we need b>3b>3. For the base case, y=0y=0, we see that v1v_{1} is a generator and 00 is clearly not in 𝒰\mathcal{U}.

For the inductive step, fix yy and assume that the lemma holds for all smaller values of yy. If 1≤y≤b1\leq y\leq b then v1+y​v2v_{1}+yv_{2} has the unique representation

v1+y​v2=(v1+(y−1)​v2)+v2.v_{1}+yv_{2}=(v_{1}+(y-1)v_{2})+v_{2}.

For b<y≤2​bb<y\leq 2b, we have the representation

v1+y​v2=(b+1)​v2+(v1+(y−b−1)​v2).v_{1}+yv_{2}=(b+1)v_{2}+(v_{1}+(y-b-1)v_{2}).

If y≡b(mod2)y\equiv b\pmod{2}, this representation is unique. Otherwise, we also have

v1+y​v2=(v1+(y−1)​v2)+v2.v_{1}+yv_{2}=(v_{1}+(y-1)v_{2})+v_{2}.

Now let 2​b<y≤3​b+22b<y\leq 3b+2. If y≡0(mod4)y\equiv 0\pmod{4}, then v1+y​v2v_{1}+y{v_{2}} has the unique representation

v1+y​v2=(v1+(y−1)​v2)+v2.v_{1}+y{v_{2}}=(v_{1}+(y-1)v_{2})+v_{2}.

If y≡−1(mod4)y\equiv-1\pmod{4}, we have the unique representation

v1+y​v2=(v1+(y−b−1)​v2)+(b+1)​v2.v_{1}+yv_{2}=(v_{1}+(y-b-1)v_{2})+(b+1)v_{2}.

If y≡1(mod4)y\equiv 1\pmod{4}, we have two representations:

v1+y​v2=(v1+(y−b−1)​v2)+(b+1)​v2=(v1+(y−1)​v2)+v2.v_{1}+y{v_{2}}=(v_{1}+(y-b-1)v_{2})+(b+1)v_{2}=(v_{1}+(y-1)v_{2})+v_{2}.

Finally, if y≡2(mod4)y\equiv 2\pmod{4} then we have no representation of v1+y​v2v_{1}+y{v_{2}}.

Continuing the induction for elements of the form y​v2yv_{2}, we see that if 1<y≤b1<y\leq b, then y​v2yv_{2} has no representation. The element v2​(b+1)=2​v1+v2v_{2}(b+1)=2v_{1}+v_{2} has the unique representation v2​(b+1)=(v1+v2)+v2v_{2}(b+1)=(v_{1}+v_{2})+v_{2}, so it is in 𝒰\mathcal{U}. The element y⁡(b+2)=(b+1)​v2+v2=(v1+2​v2)+v1y(b+2)=(b+1)v_{2}+v_{2}=(v_{1}+2v_{2})+v_{1}, however, can be expressed in two ways.

For b+2<y≤3​b−3b+2<y\leq 3b-3, we also have two representations. Precisely, if we let

i=⌊y−b−12⌋andj=⌈y−b+12⌉,i=\left\lfloor\frac{y-b-1}{2}\right\rfloor\quad\text{and}\quad j=\left\lceil\frac{y-b+1}{2}\right\rceil,

then we see that

y​v2=(v1+i​v2)+(v1+j​v2)=(v1+(i−1)​v2)+(v1+(j+1)​v2).yv_{2}=(v_{1}+iv_{2})+(v_{1}+jv_{2})=(v_{1}+(i-1)v_{2})+(v_{1}+(j+1)v_{2}).

Finally, for 3​b−2≤y≤3​b+23b-2\leq y\leq 3b+2, we have the following two representations

where we choose δ\delta to be either 11 or 22 depending on the parity of bb and yy. ∎

Proof of Theorem 4.5.

of 𝒰\mathcal{U} and take such an element with minimal NN. We consider the binary sequence (ai)(a_{i}), where ai∈ℤ/2​ℤa_{i}\in\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z} and

ai=ai−1+ai−b−1,a_{i}=a_{i-1}+a_{i-b-1},

which holds for b<i≤Nb<i\leq N. From now on, any evaluation of the aia_{i}’s will be understood to be taken modulo 22. We can now use this recursive relation to show that there are no gaps in (ai)(a_{i}) of length b+1b+1.

Precisely, we claim that, for every b≤t≤Nb\leq t\leq N, we have 1∈{at−i:0≤i≤b}1\in\{a_{t-i}:0\leq i\leq b\}. Suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that tt is a minimal counterexample. In this case, at−1=at=0a_{t-1}=a_{t}=0. Clearly, t>bt>b, so by the recursive formula we have at−b−1=at−1−at=0a_{t-b-1}=a_{t-1}-a_{t}=0, but that means that t−1t-1 is actually a smaller counterexample, which is a contradiction.

Applying this to t=Nt=N, we obtain that there is some 0≤i≤b0\leq i\leq b such that aN−i=1a_{N-i}=1. Then, by Lemma 4.6, we have the following representation of ss as the sum of two distinct elements of 𝒰\mathcal{U}:

s=(s−v1−i​v2)+(v1+i​v2).s=(s-v_{1}-iv_{2})+(v_{1}+iv_{2}).

Note that the elements are distinct because otherwise s=2​(v1+i​v2)=(b+i)​v1s=2(v_{1}+iv_{2})=(b+i)v_{1}, contradicting Lemma 4.6. Since the representation must be unique, the choice of ii is also unique. Thus, aN−j=0a_{N-j}=0 for 0≤j≤b0\leq j\leq b and j≠ij\neq i.

Using the recursive formula backwards, we can determine aN−ja_{N-j} for b<j≤2​bb<j\leq 2b. We find that aN−j=1a_{N-j}=1 if and only if j=i+b+1j=i+b+1 or j=i+bj=i+b (for i>0i>0). We now have two cases to treat separately:

Case 1: i>0i>0. In this case, both s−v1−(i+b)​v2s-v_{1}-(i+b)v_{2} and s−v1−(i+b+1)​v2s-v_{1}-(i+b+1){v_{2}} are in 𝒰\mathcal{U}. However, by Lemma 4.6, one of v1+(i+b)​v2{v_{1}}+(i+b){v_{2}} and v1+(i+b+1)​v2{v_{1}}+(i+b+1){v_{2}} is in 𝒰\mathcal{U}. Thus, we have a new representation

s=(s−v1−(i+b+δ)​v2)+(v1+(i+b+δ)​v2),s=(s-v_{1}-(i+b+\delta){v_{2}})+(v_{1}+(i+b+\delta){v_{2}}),

This, however, contradicts Lemma 4.6, so Case 1 is impossible.

Case 2: i=0i=0. This is where the proof diverges from that given by Schmerl and Spiegel [14]. Our goal is to find some k>0k>0 for which ak=aN−k=1a_{k}=a_{N-k}=1, which will give us a second representation of ss as a sum of two distinct elements of 𝒰\mathcal{U}. The recursive formula suggests arranging the aia_{i}’s into an array of height b+1b+1. This way, every number (except for the upper row) is the sum of the number to its left and the number above modulo 22. It is not surprising with this rule to see the beginning of Pascal’s triangle modulo 22 appearing. (Note that this is not the first time that it appears in the study of Ulam sets; there are similar connections in Theorem 3.3 and [2, 10].)

For b=2e⋅cb=2^{e}\cdot c for some odd value cc, these observations suggest trying to prove the following:

For 0≤q≤2e0\leq q\leq 2^{e} and 0≤r<b+10\leq r<b+1, we have

Note that, since there is no new term of the form y​v2yv_{2} by Lemma 4.6, the recursive formula we found for the sequence (ai)(a_{i}) actually holds forever. The sequence given by this recursive formula has actually already been studied, for instance in [1]. The length of its period is given by OEIS Sequence A046932.

The proof of Theorem 4.5 fails if bb is a power of two. In this case, there are infinitely many elements of the form y​v2yv_{2}. However, 𝒰\mathcal{U} is still regular, and there even exists a simple closed formula characterizing the elements of 𝒰\mathcal{U}. We can arrange the sequence (ai)(a_{i}) into an array of height b+1b+1 as before, which displays an infinite pattern as shown in Table 2.

Theorem 4.7.

For e>1e>1, let b=2eb=2^{e} and let 𝒰\mathcal{U} be the Ulam set generated by two elements, v1v_{1} and v2v_{2}, with associated lattice generated by (−2,b)(-2,b).
