We also observe that the Ulam sets with associated lattice generated by (−n,n)(-n,n), where n=2e+2n=2^{e}+2 for some integer e≥3e\geq 3, appear to be regular. In this case, we notice that there seems to be no element of the form 2​x​v1+2​y​v22xv_{1}+2yv_{2}. Moreover, based on computations, we conjecture a full characterization of all elements of the form 2​x​v1+y​v22xv_{1}+yv_{2} that are in 𝒰\mathcal{U}. In particular, we believe that 2​x​v1+y​v22xv_{1}+yv_{2} is in 𝒰\mathcal{U} if and only if

2​x​v1+y​v2=(p⁡(2e+1)​(2e+2)+q⁡(2e+2)+r)​v1+v22xv_{1}+yv_{2}=(p(2^{e}+1)(2^{e}+2)+q(2^{e}+2)+r)v_{1}+v_{2}

for some p≥0p\geq 0, 0≤q<2e+10\leq q<2^{e}+1, and 0≤r<2e+20\leq r<2^{e}+2 even, with pp, qq, and rr satisfying one of the following conditions:

  1. (1)

    q=r=0q=r=0

  2. (2)

    p=0,q=1,r=0p=0,q=1,r=0

  3. (3)

    t,q<2et,q<2^{e} and one of the following is true, where t=2e+1−rt=2^{e}+1-r.

    • •

      p=0p=0 and (q+tt)≡1(mod2){q+t\choose t}\equiv 1\pmod{2}

    • •

      p>0p>0 and q+t=2e−1q+t=2^{e}-1

    • •

      p>0p>0, q+t=2e−3q+t=2^{e}-3, and p≡1(mod4)p\equiv 1\pmod{4}

Symmetric conditions would also apply for elements of the form x​v1+2​y​v2xv_{1}+2yv_{2}. If our conjecture is correct, then any representation of the remaining elements of 𝒰\mathcal{U} of the form (2​x+1)​v1+(2​y+1)​v2(2x+1)v_{1}+(2y+1)v_{2} must use one element of the form x​v1+2​y​v2xv_{1}+2yv_{2} and one of the form 2​x​v1+y​v22xv_{1}+yv_{2}. Thus, there likely exists some full characterization of all the elements of 𝒰\mathcal{U} derivable through much detailed casework, similar to Theorem 4.7.

4.2. Keeping track of the contribution of each generator

In an Ulam set, any element decomposes uniquely as a sum of two previous elements, which themselves uniquely decompose. Repeating this process, we can therefore express any term canonically as a linear combination of the original generators. Recall that we defined the function α𝒰\alpha_{\mathcal{U}} as follows:

Definition 4.8.

Let 𝒰\mathcal{U} be an Ulam set with the generators v1v_{1} and v2v_{2}. Define the function α𝒰:𝒰→ℤ≥02\alpha_{\mathcal{U}}:\mathcal{U}\to\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{2} recursively as follows:

  • •

    Set α𝒰​(v1)=(1,0)\alpha_{\mathcal{U}}(v_{1})=(1,0), α𝒰​(v2)=(0,1)\alpha_{\mathcal{U}}(v_{2})=(0,1).

  • •

    Any other u∈𝒰u\in\mathcal{U} can be written uniquely as u=u1+u2u=u_{1}+u_{2} for some u1,u2∈𝒰u_{1},u_{2}\in\mathcal{U}. Then set α𝒰​(u)=α𝒰​(u1)+α𝒰​(u2)\alpha_{\mathcal{U}}(u)=\alpha_{\mathcal{U}}(u_{1})+\alpha_{\mathcal{U}}(u_{2}).

When the context is clear, we refer to α𝒰\alpha_{\mathcal{U}} simply as α\alpha.

If we let α⁡(u)=(α1​(u),α2​(u))\alpha(u)=(\alpha_{1}(u),\alpha_{2}(u)), it is easy to check that u=α1​(u)​v1+α2​(u)​v2u=\alpha_{1}(u)v_{1}+\alpha_{2}(u)v_{2}, as we would expect. Thus, we can recover uu from α⁡(u)\alpha(u), but α⁡(u)\alpha(u) also contains more information about how uu is formed.

Plotting α\alpha in the plane leads to a very surprising observation; asymptotically, all the points seem to cluster around a straight line passing through the origin.

Conjecture 4.9.

Let 𝒰\mathcal{U} be an Ulam set with two generators and nonzero associated lattice and let α⁡(u)=(α1​(u),α2​(u))\alpha(u)=(\alpha_{1}(u),\alpha_{2}(u)). Then there exist some number r∈ℝr\in\mathbb{R} such that, for every ε>0\varepsilon>0, we have |α1​(u)α2​(u)−r|<ε\left|\frac{\alpha_{1}(u)}{\alpha_{2}(u)}-r\right|<\varepsilon for all but finitely many u∈𝒰u\in\mathcal{U}.

This is another example of a surprising property of Ulam sets and sequences about which very little is known and it may be related to other important phenomenons such as the “hidden signal” found by Steinerberger [15] or the Rigidity Conjecture [8]. Although Conjecture 4.9 does not tell us which elements can be in the Ulam set, it tells us how each element is formed. We now prove the somewhat weaker result that the ratio α1​(u)α2​(u)\frac{\alpha_{1}(u)}{\alpha_{2}(u)} cannot be arbitrarily small or large.

Theorem 4.10.

Let the associated lattice of 𝒰\mathcal{U} be generated by (−a,b)(-a,b) and let 𝒰′\mathcal{U}^{\prime} be the image of α\alpha in ℤ≥02\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{2}. Then for every (x,y)∈𝒰′(x,y)\in\mathcal{U}^{\prime} other than (0,1)(0,1) and (1,0)(1,0), we have y≤b⁡(2​x−1)y\leq b(2x-1) and x≤a⁡(2​y−1)x\leq a(2y-1).

Proof.

Note that the only element with xx-coordinate 00 is (0,1)(0,1) while the elements (1,0),…,(1,b)(1,0),\ldots,(1,b) are in 𝒰′\mathcal{U}^{\prime}. However, (1,b+1)(1,b+1) is not included because v1+(b+1)​v2=(v1+b​v2)+v2=v1+(a​v1+v2)v_{1}+(b+1)v_{2}=(v_{1}+bv_{2})+v_{2}=v_{1}+(av_{1}+v_{2}). For y>b+1y>b+1, the only way to express (1,y)(1,y) as a sum of elements of 𝒰′\mathcal{U}^{\prime} is to use (0,1)(0,1), so we would need (1,y−1)(1,y-1) to also be in 𝒰′\mathcal{U}^{\prime}. Thus, for y>b+1y>b+1, (1,y)(1,y) is not in 𝒰′\mathcal{U}^{\prime}.

Now let’s consider the other values of xx. Since (a​v1+v2)=(b+1)​v2∈𝒰(av_{1}+v_{2})=(b+1)v_{2}\in\mathcal{U}, we cannot have more than b+1b+1 consecutive elements of 𝒰′\mathcal{U}^{\prime} in a vertical line. Indeed, if (x,y),(x,y+1),…,(x,y+b)(x,y),(x,y+1),\ldots,(x,y+b) are all in 𝒰\mathcal{U}, then (x,y+b+1)(x,y+b+1) cannot be in 𝒰\mathcal{U} because

x​v1+(y+b+1)​v2=(x​v1+(y+b)​v2)+v2=(x​v1+y​v2)+(b+1)​v2.xv_{1}+(y+b+1)v_{2}=(xv_{1}+(y+b)v_{2})+v_{2}=(xv_{1}+yv_{2})+(b+1)v_{2}.

We will now prove the result by inducting on xx. The cases x=0x=0 and x=1x=1 have already been treated, so suppose x≥2x\geq 2 and that the result holds for all smaller xx.

Assume (x,y)∈𝒰′(x,y)\in\mathcal{U}^{\prime} has the representation (x,y)=(x1,y1)+(x2,y2)(x,y)=(x_{1},y_{1})+(x_{2},y_{2}), where x1≤x2x_{1}\leq x_{2}. If x1≥1x_{1}\geq 1, then we have y1≤b⁡(2​x1−1)y_{1}\leq b(2x_{1}-1) and y2≤b⁡(2​x2−1)y_{2}\leq b(2x_{2}-1) by our inductive hypothesis, so

y=y1+y2≤b⁡(2​x−2).y=y_{1}+y_{2}\leq b(2x-2).

This means that if y>b⁡(2​x−2)y>b(2x-2), then x1=0x_{1}=0, so y1=1y_{1}=1 and (x,y−1)=(x2,y2)∈𝒰′(x,y-1)=(x_{2},y_{2})\in\mathcal{U}^{\prime}. Hence, if y=b⁡(2​x−2)+ky=b(2x-2)+k, then (x,y−1),(x,y−2),…,(x,y−k)(x,y-1),(x,y-2),\ldots,(x,y-k) are also in 𝒰\mathcal{U}. If k≥b+1k\geq b+1, then we have more than b+1b+1 consecutive elements, which is impossible as we saw earlier. Thus, k≤bk\leq b and y≤b⁡(2​x−1)y\leq b(2x-1) except for when (x,y)=(0,1)(x,y)=(0,1).

By symmetry, we also have that x≤a⁡(2​y−1)x\leq a(2y-1) except for when (x,y)=(1,0)(x,y)=(1,0), so the proof is complete. ∎

This result gives us the bounds yx≤2​b\frac{y}{x}\leq 2b and xy≤2​a\frac{x}{y}\leq 2a, which holds for all but finitely many elements.

We now focus on the case where the associated lattice is generated by (−n,n)(-n,n). This case is particularly interesting because, if Conjecture 4.9 is true, then r=1r=1 by symmetry. We note that this is the only case where there seems to be a simple expression for the exact value of rr. Moreover, we can take advantage of the symmetry to improve the bound of the previous theorem to yx<n+1\frac{y}{x}<n+1.

Theorem 4.11.

When 𝒰\mathcal{U} has associated lattice generated by (−n,n)(-n,n), then for any (x,y)∈𝒰′(x,y)\in\mathcal{U}^{\prime} other than (0,1)(0,1) and (1,0)(1,0), we have y<(n+1)​xy<(n+1)x and x<(n+1)​yx<(n+1)y.

We first require a preparatory lemma.

Lemma 4.12.

Let 𝒰\mathcal{U} have associated lattice generated by (−n,n)(-n,n). If (x,y)∈𝒰′(x,y)\in\mathcal{U}^{\prime} and x≡y(modn)x\equiv y\pmod{n}, then x=yx=y.

Proof.

By symmetry, we know that (y,x)(y,x) is in 𝒰′\mathcal{U}^{\prime}. Thus, there exists some u1,u2∈𝒰u_{1},u_{2}\in\mathcal{U} such that α⁡(u1)=(x,y)\alpha(u_{1})=(x,y) and α⁡(u2)=(y,x)\alpha(u_{2})=(y,x). But then we have

u1=x​v1+y​v2=y​v1+x​v2+(x−y)​(v1−v2)=y​v1+x​v2=u2u_{1}=xv_{1}+yv_{2}=yv_{1}+xv_{2}+(x-y)(v_{1}-v_{2})=yv_{1}+xv_{2}=u_{2}

since n|(x−y)n|(x-y). This means that (x,y)=α⁡(u1)=α⁡(u2)=(y,x)(x,y)=\alpha(u_{1})=\alpha(u_{2})=(y,x); hence x=yx=y. ∎

Proof of Theorem 4.11.

Suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that some u∈𝒰u\in\mathcal{U} other than v2v_{2} is mapped by α\alpha to (x,y)(x,y) with y≥(n+1)​xy\geq(n+1)x. Take such a uu which lexicographically minimizes (x,y)(x,y).

Since the sum of two vectors below the line y=(n+1)​xy=(n+1)x stays below the line, the representation of uu must use another element that is mapped above the line. Note that the only choice is v2v_{2}, since uu corresponds to the minimal such (x,y)(x,y). This means that u−v2u-v_{2} is in 𝒰\mathcal{U} and is mapped to (x,y−1)(x,y-1). If y−1≥(n+1)​xy-1\geq(n+1)x, then this new element contradicts the minimality of uu. Hence we must have y=(n+1)​xy=(n+1)x. But then y−x=n​xy-x=nx, so we can apply Lemma 4.12 to find that n​x=y−x=0nx=y-x=0. Thus y=x=0y=x=0, which is impossible.

A symmetric argument shows that x<(n+1)​yx<(n+1)y for (x,y)≠(1,0)(x,y)\neq(1,0). ∎

4.3. Finiteness

Although it is simple to prove, in ℤd\mathbb{Z}^{d}, that Ulam sets are always infinite (see [9]), the situation is much more complicated in ℤ×(ℤ/n​ℤ)\mathbb{Z}\times(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}). In this case, we can indeed have Ulam sets with finitely many elements. A simple example is obtained by taking the initial set S={(1,0),(1,1),…,(1,n−1)}S=\{(1,0),(1,1),\ldots,(1,n-1)\}, when n≥5n\geq 5. In this case, it is clear that no other elements outside of the initial set can be added. A more subtle example with only three generators is obtained with S={(1,0),(1,1),(2,5)}S=\{(1,0),(1,1),(2,5)\} in ℤ×(ℤ/8​ℤ)\mathbb{Z}\times(\mathbb{Z}/8\mathbb{Z}). In this example, several other elements will also be included, but if we compute enough terms, we can see that the process must terminate eventually and that there is no element with xx-coordinate greater than 5151 (see Figure 2).

This example with three generators suggests trying to find one with only two generators. Surprisingly, however, we found no finite Ulam set with two generators despite checking, with a computer, all associated lattices generated by (−a,b)(-a,b) for a,b<200a,b<200 and up to elements with x=1000x=1000.

Conjecture 4.13.

Every Ulam set in a commutative group with two generators is infinite.

Note that we can restrict our attention to ℤ×(ℤ/n​ℤ)\mathbb{Z}\times(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}) since we know that every Ulam set (in a commutative group) with two linearly dependent generators can be embedded in ℤ×(ℤ/n​ℤ)\mathbb{Z}\times(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}). Note also that this conjecture does not hold in the case of 𝒱\mathcal{V}-sets; for example, the 𝒱\mathcal{V}-set with associated lattice generated by (−3,3)(-3,3) contains only five elements.

We know, however, that when gcd⁡(a,b)=1\gcd(a,b)=1, the Ulam set with associated lattice generated by (−a,b)(-a,b) can be embedded in ℤ\mathbb{Z}, so it must be infinite. The following theorem allows us to improve this to include all cases where gcd⁡(a,b)<5\gcd(a,b)<5.

Theorem 4.14.

Let 𝒰\mathcal{U} be a finite Ulam set in ℤ×(ℤ/n​ℤ)\mathbb{Z}\times(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}) and let xmaxx_{\max} be the greatest xx-coordinate of elements of 𝒰\mathcal{U}. Then 𝒰\mathcal{U} contains at least 55 elements of the form (xmax,y)(x_{\max},y).

Proof.

If 𝒰\mathcal{U} contains a single element of the form (xmax,y)(x_{\max},y), then the sum of this element with an element of 𝒰\mathcal{U} with the second greatest xx-coordinate clearly has a unique representation, contradicting the maximality of xmaxx_{\max}.

If 𝒰\mathcal{U} contains two or three elements of this form, then the sum of any two of them again has a unique representation and greater xx-coordinate.

Now suppose that 𝒰\mathcal{U} contains four elements of this form: u1u_{1}, u2u_{2}, u3u_{3}, and u4u_{4}. Then the only possible second representation of u1+u2u_{1}+u_{2} is u3+u4u_{3}+u_{4}, so u1+u2=u3+u4u_{1}+u_{2}=u_{3}+u_{4}. Similarly, u1+u3=u2+u4u_{1}+u_{3}=u_{2}+u_{4} and u1+u4=u2+u3u_{1}+u_{4}=u_{2}+u_{3}. Thus, we have the following system of equations:

{u1+u2=u3+u4u1+u3=u2+u4u1+u4=u2+u3\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}u_{1}+u_{2}=u_{3}+u_{4}\\ u_{1}+u_{3}=u_{2}+u_{4}\\ u_{1}+u_{4}=u_{2}+u_{3}\end{array}\right.

Subtracting the first two equations yields u2−u3=u3−u2u_{2}-u_{3}=u_{3}-u_{2}, so 2​u2=2​u32u_{2}=2u_{3}. Similarly we can obtain 2​ui=2​uj2u_{i}=2u_{j} for all pairs i,j∈{1,2,3,4}i,j\in\{1,2,3,4\}. If nn is odd, then ui=uju_{i}=u_{j} (because then 22 if invertible modulo nn), which is impossible. If nn is even then it only forces ui∈{uj,uj+(0,n2)}u_{i}\in\{u_{j},u_{j}+(0,\frac{n}{2})\}. This means, however, that for every i∈{1,2,3,4}i\in\{1,2,3,4\}, uiu_{i} is either equal to u1u_{1} or u1+(0,n2)u_{1}+(0,\frac{n}{2}). Since the four uiu_{i}’s are different and there are only two choices, this is also impossible. Hence, there must be at least 55 elements of the form (xmax,y)(x_{\max},y). ∎

Corollary 4.15.

All Ulam sets in ℤ×(ℤ/2​ℤ)\mathbb{Z}\times(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}), ℤ×(ℤ/3​ℤ)\mathbb{Z}\times(\mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z}) and ℤ×(ℤ/4​ℤ)\mathbb{Z}\times(\mathbb{Z}/4\mathbb{Z}) are infinite.

Proof.

Since there are less than 55 possible values of yy, the condition of Theorem 4.14 cannot be fulfilled, so the Ulam sets must be infinite. ∎

5. Higher-dimensional 𝒱\mathcal{V}-sets

In this section, we study 𝒱\mathcal{V}-sets, the variant of Ulam sets where we don’t require the summands in the representations to be distinct. These sets share many properties with Ulam sets. In particular, Conjecture 4.9 appears to also hold in the case of 𝒱\mathcal{V}-sets. Moreover, the properties pertaining to associated lattices, discussed at the beginning of Section 4, still apply to 𝒱\mathcal{V}-sets.

The case of 𝒱\mathcal{V}-sequences (in ℤ\mathbb{Z}) have already been studied by Kuca [10], so we focus on 𝒱\mathcal{V}-sets in ℤ2\mathbb{Z}^{2}.

5.1. The column phenomenon

In Section 3.3, we extended the column phenomenon first observed by Kravitz and Steinerberger [9] to a noncommutative setting. We will now prove a generalization of this phenomenon in commutative settings that will allow us to extend it to 𝒱\mathcal{V}-sets.

Definition 5.1.

If SS is a subset of ℤ≥02\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{2}, we say that the xx-column is eventually periodic with period pp when, for a sufficiently large yy, (x,y)∈S(x,y)\in S if and only if (x,y+p)∈S(x,y+p)\in S.

Kravitz and Steinerberger proved that if an Ulam set in ℤ2\mathbb{Z}^{2} has a single generator lying on the first column (x=0x=0), then all of the columns are eventually periodic.

For 𝒱\mathcal{V}-sets, however, a single generator (0,a)(0,a) in the first column will generate a full sequence of points in this column: (0,2​a)(0,2a), (0,3​a)(0,3a), (0,5​a)(0,5a), (0,7​a)(0,7a), (0,9​a)(0,9a), and so on. The periodic behavior in the first column suggests the following generalization:

Theorem 5.2.

Let 𝒮\mathcal{S} either be an Ulam set or a 𝒱\mathcal{V}-set in ℤ2\mathbb{Z}^{2} for which the column x=0x=0 is eventually periodic. Then all the columns of 𝒮\mathcal{S} are eventually periodic.

Proof.

We proceed by inducting on xx. Fix some x>0x>0 and suppose that all previous columns are eventually periodic. Let PP be the least common multiple of their periods.

We will need to count the number of representations of (x,y)(x,y) as sums of previous elements. Moreover, since the exact number of representations does not matter once there is more than one, we will encode the number of representations with a symbol in {0,1,2+}\{0,1,2_{+}\} (as in Theorem 3.9), where the symbols 00 and 11 mean there are 00 and 11 representations, respectively, and 2+2_{+} means there are two or more representations. Finally, when we count representations, we can either require the summands to be distinct or not require this restriction, depending on whether we are working with an Ulam set or a 𝒱\mathcal{V}-set. The proof works equally well in both settings.

We first ignore the first column and define by∈{0,1,2+}b_{y}\in\{0,1,2_{+}\} to be the number of representations of (x,y)(x,y) as a sum of elements from the other columns. We show that byb_{y} is eventually periodic with period PP.

Indeed, suppose that we have a representation (x,y)=(x1,y1)+(x2,y2)(x,y)=(x_{1},y_{1})+(x_{2},y_{2}), with y1≤y2y_{1}\leq y_{2}. It is clear that, for sufficiently large yy, the point (x2,y2)(x_{2},y_{2}) must come from the periodic section of its column. If (x1,y1)(x_{1},y_{1}) also does, then we have another representation (x,y)=(x1,y1−P)+(x2,y2+P)(x,y)=(x_{1},y_{1}-P)+(x_{2},y_{2}+P), so by=2+b_{y}=2_{+}. Similarly by+P=2+b_{y+P}=2_{+} because (x,y+P)=(x1,y1)+(x2,y2+P)(x,y+P)=(x_{1},y_{1})+(x_{2},y_{2}+P). Furthermore, if (x,y+P)(x,y+P) has such a representation, then (x,y)(x,y) also does and we again have by=by+P=2+b_{y}=b_{y+P}=2_{+}.

Now, suppose all representations of both (x,y)(x,y) and (x,y+p)(x,y+p) use an element from the non-periodic transient phase of its column. Then any representation (x,y)=(x1,y1)+(x2,y2)(x,y)=(x_{1},y_{1})+(x_{2},y_{2}) yields the representation (x,y+P)=(x1,y1)+(x2,y2+P)(x,y+P)=(x_{1},y_{1})+(x_{2},y_{2}+P). Similarly, a representation of (x,y+P)(x,y+P) yields one for (x,y)(x,y). We therefore have a bijection between representations of (x,y)(x,y) and (x,y+P)(x,y+P), which shows that by=by+Pb_{y}=b_{y+P}.

We now need to split the first column into its finite transient phase and its infinite periodic section. Since its minimal period divides PP, for any congruence class modulo PP, either (0,y)∈𝒮(0,y)\in\mathcal{S} for all sufficiently large yy in this equivalence class, or (0,y)∉𝒮(0,y)\not\in\mathcal{S} for all sufficiently large yy in this equivalence class. Let CC be the set of congruence classes modulo PP that contain the values yy for which (0,y)(0,y) is eventually always in 𝒮\mathcal{S}, and let TT be the finite set of elements of 𝒮\mathcal{S} not in one of these classes.

Let cy∈{0,1,2+}c_{y}\in\{0,1,2_{+}\} be the number of representations of (x,y)(x,y), where we now also take into account the infinite periodic section of the first column.

For a congruence class R∈ℤ/P​ℤR\in\mathbb{Z}/P\mathbb{Z}, consider the congruence classes R−SR-S for S∈CS\in C. Then each y′y^{\prime} in one of those classes with (x,y′)∈𝒮(x,y^{\prime})\in\mathcal{S} yields a representation of (x,y)(x,y) for all sufficiently large y∈Ry\in R. Thus, if there are two or more such elements, cy=2+c_{y}=2_{+} for all sufficiently large y∈Ry\in R. If there is one such element, then cy=by+1c_{y}=b_{y}+1 for all sufficiently large y∈Ry\in R, and if there is no such element then cy=byc_{y}=b_{y}. Thus, the sequence (cy)(c_{y}) is still eventually periodic with period PP.

All that’s left for us to consider is the effect of TT, the set of elements in the non-periodic transient phase of the first column. Let aya_{y} be the indicator sequence for the elements of the xx-column (ay=1a_{y}=1 if (x,y)∈𝒮(x,y)\in\mathcal{S} and ay=0a_{y}=0 otherwise). It is clear that the sequence (ay)(a_{y}) is determined by cyc_{y} and TT recursively as follows:

If cy=0c_{y}=0 and there exists a unique t∈Tt\in T for which ay−t=1a_{y-t}=1, then ay=1a_{y}=1. If cy=1c_{y}=1 and there exists no t∈Tt\in T for which ay−t=1a_{y-t}=1, then ay=1a_{y}=1. Otherwise, ay=0a_{y}=0.

Let mm be the maximal element of TT. Then, for sufficiently large yy, aya_{y} is uniquely determined by ay−1,ay−2,…,ay−ma_{y-1},a_{y-2},\ldots,a_{y-m} and the residue of yy modulo PP. However, since there are only 2m2^{m} possible combinations of values for ai−1,ai−2,…,ai−ma_{i-1},a_{i-2},\ldots,a_{i-m}, there must eventually be some y0y_{0} and k>0k>0 such that ay0−j=ay0+k​P−ja_{y_{0}-j}=a_{y_{0}+kP-j} for all 1≤j≤m1\leq j\leq m. But since ay0a_{y_{0}} depends solely on ay0−1,…​ay0−ma_{y_{0}-1},\ldots a_{y_{0}-m}, we must also have ay0=ay0−k​Pa_{y_{0}}=a_{y_{0}-kP}. Continuing to apply the recursive relation therefore implies that aya_{y} is eventually periodic (when y≥y0y\geq y_{0}) with period k​PkP. ∎

Note that our proof only provides large bounds on the periods of the columns. Indeed, the period could increase by a factor of up to 2m2^{m} whenever xx increases by 11. If TT contains a single element tt (as in the case of 𝒱\mathcal{V}-sets with a single generator on the yy-axis), then we can actually improve this bound and show that the period at most doubles when xx increases by 11 (consider each congruence class modulo tt separately in the third part of the proof). In many cases, however, this doubling rarely occurs, as noted in [9] for the case of Ulam sets. It would therefore be interesting to try to obtain better bounds on the periods.

5.2. The 𝒱\mathcal{V}-set with two independent generators

Contrary to the case of Ulam sets, the 𝒱\mathcal{V}-set on two generators with associated lattice zero does not have a nice simple lattice structure. We can, however, obtain an interesting result about the structure of this 𝒱\mathcal{V}-set, which we will consider to be embedded in ℤ2\mathbb{Z}^{2} with initial set {(0,1),(1,0)}\{(0,1),(1,0)\} (since all 𝒱\mathcal{V}-sets with linearly independent generators are structurally equivalent to this one). For simplicity, we will refer to 𝒱⁡({(0,1),(1,0)})\mathcal{V}(\{(0,1),(1,0)\}) simply as 𝒱0\mathcal{V}_{0}.

Theorem 5.3.

Let EE be the set of elements (x,y)(x,y) such that (x,y)≡(0,1),(0,3),(1,0),(3,0)(x,y)\equiv(0,1),(0,3),(1,0),(3,0) or (2,2)(mod4)(2,2)\pmod{4}. Then all the elements of 𝒱0\mathcal{V}_{0} are in EE except (1,1)(1,1), (2,0)(2,0), (0,2)(0,2), (3,2)(3,2), (2,3)(2,3), (6,3)(6,3), (3,6)(3,6), (9,6)(9,6), (6,9)(6,9), (10,5)(10,5), (5,10)(5,10), (14,5)(14,5), and (5,14)(5,14).

Proof.

According to Theorem 5.2, all the columns are eventually periodic. We will need to explicitly compute the elements of the first 1212 columns of 𝒱0\mathcal{V}_{0}:

  • •

    (0,y)∈𝒱0⇔y≡1(mod2)(0,y)\in\mathcal{V}_{0}\iff y\equiv 1\pmod{2} or y=2y=2

  • •

    (1,y)∈𝒱0⇔y≡0(mod4)(1,y)\in\mathcal{V}_{0}\iff y\equiv 0\pmod{4} or y=1y=1

  • •

    (2,y)∈𝒱0⇔y≡2(mod4)(2,y)\in\mathcal{V}_{0}\iff y\equiv 2\pmod{4} and y≥6y\geq 6 or y∈{0,3}y\in\{0,3\}

  • •

    (3,y)∈𝒱0⇔y≡0(mod4)(3,y)\in\mathcal{V}_{0}\iff y\equiv 0\pmod{4} and y≥12y\geq 12 or y∈{0,2,6}y\in\{0,2,6\}

  • •

    (4,y)∈𝒱0⇔y∈{1,7}(4,y)\in\mathcal{V}_{0}\iff y\in\{1,7\}

  • •

    (5,y)∈𝒱0⇔y∈{0,10,14}(5,y)\in\mathcal{V}_{0}\iff y\in\{0,10,14\}

  • •

    (6,y)∈𝒱0⇔y∈{2,3,9}(6,y)\in\mathcal{V}_{0}\iff y\in\{2,3,9\}

  • •

    (7,y)∈𝒱0⇔y∈{0,4,16}(7,y)\in\mathcal{V}_{0}\iff y\in\{0,4,16\}

  • •

    (8,y)∈𝒱0⇔y≡3(mod4)(8,y)\in\mathcal{V}_{0}\iff y\equiv 3\pmod{4} and y≥19y\geq 19 or y∈{1,13}y\in\{1,13\}

  • •

    (9,y)∈𝒱0⇔y≡0(mod4)(9,y)\in\mathcal{V}_{0}\iff y\equiv 0\pmod{4} and y≥16y\geq 16 or y∈{0,6}y\in\{0,6\}

  • •

    (10,y)∈𝒱0⇔y∈{2,5}(10,y)\in\mathcal{V}_{0}\iff y\in\{2,5\}

  • •

    (11,y)∈𝒱0⇔y=0(11,y)\in\mathcal{V}_{0}\iff y=0

It is just a matter of computation to check that this does hold. Note that we have symmetric results since everything still holds when we swap xx and yy. Now we split the proof into three parts.

First, we show that 𝒱0\mathcal{V}_{0} contains no point with both odd xx and odd yy, except (1,1)(1,1). If xx and yy are both odd, we have (x,y)=(x,0)+(0,y)(x,y)=(x,0)+(0,y). Now write x=4​k1+r1x=4k_{1}+r_{1} and y=4​k2+r2y=4k_{2}+r_{2}, with r1,r2∈{1,3}r_{1},r_{2}\in\{1,3\}. If k1≤2k_{1}\leq 2 or k2≤2k_{2}\leq 2, then (x,y)(x,y) is in one of the first 1212 columns or one of the first 1212 rows of 𝒱0\mathcal{V}_{0}. This case has already been dealt with. If k1,k2>3k_{1},k_{2}>3, however, we have another representation (x,y)=(r1,4​k2)+(4​k1,r2)(x,y)=(r_{1},4k_{2})+(4k_{1},r_{2}). Thus, (x,y)(x,y) cannot be in 𝒱0\mathcal{V}_{0}.

Second, we now show that 𝒱0\mathcal{V}_{0} contains no elements with both coordinates even and with at least one of the coordinates divisible by 44, except (0,2)(0,2) and (2,0)(2,0). By symmetry, we can assume without loss of generality that xx is divisible by 44, so (x,y)=(4​ℓ,2​k)(x,y)=(4\ell,2k) for some ℓ\ell and kk. Suppose that ℓ>2\ell>2 and k>1k>1 (otherwise (x,y)(x,y) is in one of the first 1212 columns). Then we have two distinct representations

(x,y)=(4​ℓ,1)+(0,2​k−1)=(4​ℓ,3)+(0,2​k−3).(x,y)=(4\ell,1)+(0,2k-1)=(4\ell,3)+(0,2k-3).

Hence (x,y)(x,y) is not in 𝒱0\mathcal{V}_{0}.

Third, we show that 𝒱0\mathcal{V}_{0} contains no point with xx odd and y≡2(mod4)y\equiv 2\pmod{4}, except (3,2)(3,2), (3,6)(3,6), (5,10)(5,10), (5,14)(5,14), and (9,6)(9,6). Once again, suppose that x,y≥12x,y\geq 12. Then we have two distinct representations

(x,y)=(x−2,0)+(2,y)=(x−d,2)+(d,y−2),(x,y)=(x-2,0)+(2,y)=(x-d,2)+(d,y-2),

where d=1d=1 if x≡3(mod4)x\equiv 3\pmod{4} and d=3d=3 if x≡1(mod4)x\equiv 1\pmod{4}. Hence, (x,y)(x,y) is not in 𝒱0\mathcal{V}_{0}. By symmetry, we also have that 𝒱0\mathcal{V}_{0} contains no element with odd yy and x≡2(mod4)x\equiv 2\pmod{4} except for (2,3)(2,3), (6,3)(6,3), (10,5)(10,5), (14,5)(14,5), (6,9)(6,9).

Combining these three results, we see that the only combinations of remainders modulo 44 for xx and yy that have not been excluded are (0,1),(0,3),(1,0),(3,0)(0,1),(0,3),(1,0),(3,0) and (2,2)(2,2), so all the elements of 𝒱0\mathcal{V}_{0} except for the few listed exceptions are in one of these classes. ∎

This is very similar to the condition in Theorem 4.2: it is indeed easy to check that the sum of two elements in EE is never in EE. Our result therefore implies that there is some finite set T⊂𝒱0T\subset\mathcal{V}_{0} such that the representation of sufficiently large elements in 𝒱0\mathcal{V}_{0} necessarily uses a summand from TT.

Corollary 5.4.

Let

T={(1,1),(2,0),(0,2),(3,2),(2,3),(6,3),(3,6),(9,6),(6,9),(10,5),(5,10),(14,5),(5,14)}.T=\{(1,1),(2,0),(0,2),(3,2),(2,3),(6,3),(3,6),(9,6),(6,9),(10,5),(5,10),(14,5),(5,14)\}.

Then every element of 𝒱⁡({(0,1),(1,0)})\mathcal{V}(\{(0,1),(1,0)\}) outside of TT (and the generators) must use an element of TT in its (unique) representation as a sum of two previous elements.

Proof.

This follows directly from Theorem 5.3 and the fact that the sum of two elements in EE is never in EE. ∎

Even though this is enough to imply regularity in one dimension (Theorem 4.2), it is unfortunately not necessarily the case in higher dimensions, and the structure of 𝒱0\mathcal{V}_{0} still appears to be quite hard to describe. Theorem 5.2 implies that the columns and rows are eventually periodic, but the transient phases seem to be too long for a lattice structure to emerge.

We believe that Corollary 5.4 could help prove that 𝒱0\mathcal{V}_{0} has positive asymptotic density, which would be an interesting result for a 𝒱\mathcal{V}-set with no lattice structure. It has also allowed us to efficiently compute, with a computer, all the elements of 𝒱0\mathcal{V}_{0} with xx and yy up to 5000050000. These computations showed that the density empirically seems to be approximately 0.12180.1218 (density of 0.059080.05908 for the points of type (0,1)/(1,0)(0,1)/(1,0), 0.059590.05959 for those of type (0,3)/(3,0)(0,3)/(3,0) and 0.003140.00314 for those of type (2,2)(2,2)). Note that the points of type (2,2)(2,2) are much rarer than the other types.

6. Conclusion and open problems

We conclude by gathering a few open questions that arose during the present investigation.

6.1. Complete characterization of elements in 𝒰⁡({0,1})\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\})

We fully characterized all terms in 𝒰⁡({0,1})\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}) with exactly one 11 (and, by Theorem 3.1, those with exactly one 00). We also investigated symmetries (reverses, bit-wise complements, and palindromes) and general conditions for words with exactly two 11’s. However, the full characterization of all words in 𝒰⁡({0,1})\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}) still remains unsolved. In Theorem 3.3, we found that the condition for a word with one 11 to be in the Ulam set is a modular restriction of a binomial coefficient. We predict that a similar modular restriction must suffice for a binomial coefficient or sum of binomial coefficients that correspond to a word with more than one 11.

In particular, finding the exact number of words of length nn in 𝒰⁡({0,1})\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}) and the asymptotic density of the Ulam set (Conjecture 3.10) remains an interesting problem for future research.

6.2. Ulam sets in matrix groups

The idea of Ulam sets arising from non-abelian settings can be extended to matrices, where we use the determinant of a matrix as our notion of size. To ensure that this notion is suitable for generating an Ulam set, our starting matrices must have determinants greater than 11. The generating matrices must also not commute.

If the generating matrices are such that every matrix representable as a product of the starting matrices must have a unique representation, then any matrix can be represented uniquely as a word on the alphabet containing the starting matrices. Hence, the Ulam set on two generators in the matrix setting would be isomorphic to 𝒰⁡({0,1}).\mathcal{U}(\{0,1\}). Therefore, Ulam sets in matrix groups extend the study of Ulam sets in free groups. Matrices allow us to add new conditions on our set; we focus on the case where there is a relation between the generating matrices that would allow for a matrix to have a non-unique representation as the product of the starting generators. In particular, the Ulam set 𝒰⁡({A,B})\mathcal{U}(\{A,B\}), where

A=(04−44)andB=(08−80)A=\begin{pmatrix}0&4\\ -4&4\end{pmatrix}\quad\text{and}\quad B=\begin{pmatrix}0&8\\ -8&0\end{pmatrix}

satisfy A3=B2A^{3}=B^{2}, is an interesting area for future investigation.

6.3. Decomposition into sums or products of the generators

We believe that the function α\alpha keeping track of the contribution of each generator to an element could be very important for a better understanding of Ulam sets. In particular, in commutative settings, further work on Conjecture 4.9 stating that the ratio α1α2\frac{\alpha_{1}}{\alpha_{2}} stabilizes might be interesting. A first step toward this conjecture would be to improve the bounds on α1α2\frac{\alpha_{1}}{\alpha_{2}} given by Theorems 4.10 and 4.11.

Note that we can define a similar α\alpha function in noncommutative settings. The ratio does not necessarily seem to stabilize in this case, but we believe that it is still possible to bound it in some cases. In particular, for Ulam sets of matrices where the only relation between the two generators AA and BB is A3=B2A^{3}=B^{2}, we believe that αAαB≥1\frac{\alpha_{A}}{\alpha_{B}}\geq 1 for all elements except the generator BB itself. There also seems to be an infinite class of matrices in this Ulam set satisfying αAαB=1\frac{\alpha_{A}}{\alpha_{B}}=1. Further research on the noncommutative version of this phenomenon could also be enlightening.

6.4. Regularity conjecture

We conjectured that, for even a≥2a\geq 2 and sufficiently large bb (depending on aa), the Ulam set with associated lattice generated by (−a,b)(-a,b) is always regular. We settled the case a=2a=2 with Theorems 4.5 and 4.7, and the case with a=4a=4 and b≡1(mod4)b\equiv 1\pmod{4} has already been solved in [2]. We believe that similar work could be applied for other small cases, but new methods will likely be necessary for the general case. Since proofs of regularity appear to often require a lot of casework, we think that computer-assisted proofs may be helpful for further advances.

Note also that we focused mostly on Ulam sets but that we observed regularity for many 𝒱\mathcal{V}-sets in ℤ×(ℤ/n​ℤ)\mathbb{Z}\times(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}) as well. A deeper study of these cases could bring a better understanding of regularity phenomenons.

6.5. Better conditions for finiteness

Another interesting path for further research is the characterization of finite Ulam sets based on their sets of generators. We conjectured that Ulam sets with two generators (in commutative groups) cannot be finite. Any new partial result on this conjecture would be quite interesting. Moreover, we studied finiteness only in commutative groups, but this could also be studied in the noncommutative case.

6.6. Density of each row in ℤ×(ℤ/n​ℤ)\mathbb{Z}\times(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})

We observed that, in general, the elements of Ulam sets in ℤ×(ℤ/n​ℤ)\mathbb{Z}\times(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}) are not equally distributed between the different rows (values of yy). For example, if we take n=3n=3 and initial set {(1,1),(1,2)}\{(1,1),(1,2)\}, then there are very few points in the Ulam set with yy-coordinate 00, compared to y=1y=1 or y=2y=2. Studying this phenomenon deeper could be a promising avenue for future research.
